Article Title: Ferrari’s first all-electric car sells for $40 million at charity auction, nearly 40 times initial estimate of $1.1 million; buyer won’t receive it until 2027
Article Text:
Ferrari’s Luce “Chassis 0” sets a new auction record after selling for $40 million at charity auction.

Ferrari Luce breaks previous $26 million record

Ferrari Luce packs four electric motors, 1,050 cv of power, a 310 km/h top speed and a 530 km claimed range.

What makes the $40 million Ferrari Luce special?

With a 122 kWh battery, 800V architecture and 1,050 cv, Ferrari’s Luce accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h in just 2.5 seconds.

Ferrari Luce packs more than 1,000 horsepower

Ferrari’s Luce brings supercar performance to its first EV.

Ferrari aims to make its EV feel like a Ferrari

Ferrari’s first all-electric vehicle has made history even before reaching its buyer. A bespoke 2026 Ferrari Luce, identified as “Chassis 0” and described as the first production chassis from the Luce programme, sold for exactly $40 million at an RM Sotheby’s charity auction in Monterey on Saturday.As Road & Track reported, the record-breaking sale makes the electric Ferrari the most expensive new car ever sold at auction. The auction house waived its buyer’s premium, meaning the entire $40 million will go to The Ferrari Foundation, which plans to use the proceeds for future educational initiatives.Despite the eye-watering sale price, the buyer will not take delivery of the car until the first quarter of 2027. The vehicle is expected to return to Ferrari’s headquarters in Maranello before being delivered.The $40 million sale surpassed the previous record set in 2025, when a customised Ferrari Daytona SP3 sold for $26 million at auction.The Luce’s result is particularly notable given the criticism Ferrari faced from some traditionalists following the unveiling of its first fully electric model. Ferrari introduced the Luce in May with a starting price of €550,000, or around $636,356.The vehicle represents a major departure from Ferrari’s traditional combustion-engine sports cars. The model was designed in collaboration with LoveFrom, the design studio founded by former Apple design chief Jony Ive.The auction car was created through Ferrari’s Tailor Made programme and was designed around the theme of light. Its bespoke exterior is finished in Madreperla Semi-Gloss, featuring a dedicated pigment that shifts between green and violet depending on the angle and intensity of the light.Inside, the cabin is upholstered in Perla Le Mans metallic leather made from selected Swiss hides. Other interior elements that would typically be black have been finished in Grigio Corvara.The car also features bespoke wheels, customised brake calipers and a Ferrari logo set against an optical-white background. Ferrari says the complexity of the paint application means that no two examples will look exactly alike.However, the biggest distinction is its “Chassis 0” status. Ferrari describes it as the first production chassis of the Luce programme, giving the buyer a unique piece of the marque’s electric-car history.According to Ferrari’s official website, the Luce is powered by four electric motors, with one motor driving each wheel. The powertrain produces 1,050 cv and allows the car to accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h in 2.5 seconds.The electric four-door has a claimed top speed of 310 km/h and a range of 530 kilometres on a full charge. It uses a 122 kWh battery pack, an 800-volt electrical architecture and weighs 2,260 kilograms.Ferrari describes the Luce as a spacious hatchback capable of seating five people.The vehicle uses a new vehicle control unit designed to network its various systems, with targets updated 200 times per second. The front motors produce 210 kW at the axle, while the rear motors generate 620 kW.Ferrari has also focused heavily on preserving the driving character associated with its combustion-engine models.The Luce features a separate elastically mounted subframe, which Ferrari says is a first for the brand and helps reduce unwanted vibrations. A precision accelerometer at the centre of the rear axle monitors the natural frequencies of rotating components.Ferrari says those frequencies are then processed to create a sound reminiscent of the brand’s traditional engines, using an approach similar to that of an electric guitar.The car also features a Torque Shift Engagement system designed to progressively deliver torque during cornering. An e-manettino manages power, torque curves, traction and performance through Range, Tour and Performance settings.Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna said after the car’s unveiling that the Luce had attracted orders from both existing and new customers.“The Ferrari Luce has nothing to do with electric cars you have seen from other players,” Vigna said in May, adding that customers would need to see and drive the car to understand how distinct its design, performance and interior are.With its $40 million charity-auction sale, the Ferrari Luce has now secured a place in automotive history before its first customer delivery.
Article Summary: A bespoke 2026 Ferrari Luce sold for exactly $40 million at an RM Sotheby’s charity auction in Monterey on Saturday. The sale makes the electric Ferrari the most expensive new car ever sold at auction. Despite the eye-watering sale price, the buyer will not take delivery of the car until the first quarter of 2027.

Article Title: 'Not worthy of life': Israel minister Ben-Gvir calls for killing '30 to 40' people daily in Gaza
Article Text:
Ben-Gvir calls for more Gaza killings

Israeli national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, a lawmaker in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ’s coalition, publicly called for the killing of “30 to 40” people in Gaza each night, in comments that surfaced on Sunday.“It’s no secret, I disagree with the prime minister," he said. “I think targeted assassinations should be carried out in Gaza, taking down 30 to 40 every night. Not just those who pose an immediate threat — there are people there who are not worthy of life. They shouldn’t live. They’re not even people.”Ben-Gvir made the remarks during a conversation with Rom Braslavski, a former Gaza hostage, on Braslavski’s podcast. The discussion centred on Israel’s recovery from the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, when Ben-Gvir criticised what he described as a recent reduction in Israeli strikes on Gaza.Similar remarks by Ben-Gvir and other Israeli officials have previously drawn widespread condemnation and have been cited at the UN’s International Court of Justice as evidence of alleged genocidal intent. Israel has denied allegations that it is committing genocide in Gaza.Ben-Gvir does not control Israel’s military and has no authority to order strikes on Gaza. However, after spending decades on the far-right fringes of Israeli politics, he has emerged as one of the country’s most influential figures.He oversees key parts of Israel’s security apparatus, including the national police and the prison service, which holds thousands of Palestinians from Gaza and the West Bank. Ben-Gvir has previously boasted about reducing food rations for Palestinian prisoners.In 2025, Israel’s top court ruled that the prison service under his leadership was depriving Palestinian inmates of the minimum food required for subsistence.Until recently, Israel had been carrying out near-daily strikes on Gaza, with more than 1,250 people killed since an October truce took effect, according to Gaza’s health ministry.The Israeli military says the strikes have targeted Hamas militants. The attacks appeared to ease in recent days in what was seen as a quiet concession to US President Donald Trump, after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the president’s latest push to advance the truce, as cited by news agency AP.Trump’s latest proposal calls for Hamas to gradually surrender its weapons, while Israeli forces halt attacks and begin withdrawing from Gaza.Hamas has accepted the plan, but has tied the surrender of its heaviest weapons to the establishment of a Palestinian state, a prospect firmly rejected by Israel’s current government and much of its political establishment.Netanyahu has said Israel will not withdraw from Gaza or alter its position until Hamas is completely disarmed. The deadlock has left other elements of the proposed ceasefire, including the deployment of an international force and plans to rebuild the war-ravaged territory, on hold.
Article Summary: Itamar Ben-Gvir, a lawmaker in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ’s coalition, publicly called for the killing of ‘30 to 40’ people in Gaza each night. He made the remarks during a conversation with Rom Braslavski, a former Gaza hostage.

Article Title: Europe wildfires: 2 dead, 500 evacuated as twin blazes hit Greek island near Athens
Article Text:
Two people have died in fires that broke out simultaneously Sunday on the island of Salamis near Athens, the local fire department said. (Photo: @CGTNOfficial)

200 firefighters try to keep Salamina fires apart

Belgium fire burns 30 sq km in High Fens

European countries send aircraft, helicopters

France evacuates 650 as fires spread across region

UK battles 14 wildfires as blazes hit Germany, Croatia

Two wildfires that broke out minutes apart on the Greek island of Salamina on Sunday killed two people and prompted the evacuation of about 500 people by sea, as crews raced to prevent the fires from joining.The emergency began at 2.40pm local time in Peristeria in the island's south, where strong winds pushed flames through a wooded residential area. About 20 minutes later, another fire was reported in the eastern town of Selinia. Officials had not established the cause of either blaze.About 37,000 people live on Salamina, west of Athens, and many of them are elderly. Authorities had placed the island at high wildfire risk on Sunday as winds approached gale force.“These conditions enabled the fire to quickly reach dangerous proportions and spread rapidly within seven minutes toward nearby residential areas,” fire brigadier general Vasileios Vathrakogiannis said, news agency AP reported.Fire crews found two bodies in Peristeria.The local mayor told Greek media that the dead were believed to be a couple. Greek health minister Adonis Georgiades said on X that at least 10 others had burns or showed “symptoms of smoke inhalation”.Five were taken for treatment locally.Firefighters were deployed across Salamina, backed by 50 fire engines, aircraft, water tankers and construction machinery. Deputy mayor Thodoris Zannis said crews were trying to stop the fires from spreading over a mountain and joining to form a single blaze.About 500 people, including beachgoers, were evacuated by sea. Firefighting and coast guard vessels joined the operation, while five patrol boats and several private vessels were also sent to assist.One of the fires was under control and the evacuation operation had ended by Sunday evening, according to Greek media. Crews were still dealing with scattered fires around Peristeria late on Sunday, while officials said the Selinia blaze had “no active front”.Two coast guard vessels and a fire department vessel were to stay in the area to provide assistance and keep watch.The fires on Salamina were part of a wider outbreak across Europe over the weekend, with crews also battling major blazes in Belgium, France, the UK, Germany and Croatia.By Sunday, the fire in eastern Belgium's High Fens, or Hautes Fagnes, had burned about 30 sq km, making it one of the country's worst wildfires in recent history. Crews were on their third day of operations in Belgium's largest nature reserve, where the affected area had more than doubled within 24 hours, BBC reported.The 30 sq km burned was already more than twice the nearly 14 sq km lost in a 2011 fire in the same area, which had previously been Belgium's largest wildfire on record, according to European Forest Fire Information System data.Shifting winds and spreading smoke prompted authorities on Saturday to order about 600 residents of Waimes and Butgenbach, in Liege province near the German border, to leave their homes. Tourists were advised to leave as well, and a nearby gymnasium was opened to accommodate evacuees.More than 250 emergency personnel were involved in the response, Liege provincial governor Herve Jamar said. They included over 100 firefighters from Belgium and Germany, along with police, military personnel and civil protection staff. Helicopters operated by Belgium's federal police and the Netherlands also supported the operation.Weeks of unusually hot and dry weather had left conditions difficult for crews, with the High Fens' heathland and peat bogs adding to the challenge. Nicolas Yernaux, a spokesperson for the Public Service of Wallonia, pointed to the dryness of the ground. “We’re dealing with something much deeper because we have very dry soil,” he said.The fire was still advancing on Sunday in terrain that crews found difficult to reach, according to Rene Dahmen, chief engineer at the Department of Nature and Forest. “On the eastern flank, there’s a line at least a kilometer long where the fire is slowly advancing toward a municipal forest,” Dahmen said. “That’s the first priority now.”Belgian interior minister Bernard Quintin said on X that firefighters had stopped the fire from spreading westwards and towards the German town of Monschau. German authorities said it was about 1.5km from the border on Sunday.Farmers on both sides of the Belgium-Germany border also assisted, using tanker trucks filled with water pumped from a nearby lake before heading towards the fire zone.Belgium had experienced another period of intense heat during the week, with temperatures in parts of the country reaching about 37°C on Friday.Belgium sought international assistance by activating the European Union's civil protection mechanism, EU commissioner for crisis management, with Hadja Lahbib saying “The High Fens are burning. Belgium is not facing it alone,” on X.Sweden provided two water-bombing aircraft. Three helicopters were also being sent — two from the Netherlands and one from the Czech Republic.In southwestern France, about 17 sq km had burned in a pine forest in the Landes region and roughly 650 people had been evacuated. Landes prefect Gilles Clavreul said firefighters encountered no major flare-ups overnight.The Landes fire was the third major blaze in the pine forests of southwestern France this summer, after two others in late July.Elsewhere in the southwest, a fire in neighbouring Gironde department burned about 420 sq km and led authorities to evacuate around 220,000 people as the flames moved towards the Atlantic coast and the Bordeaux area.In the UK, military personnel were supporting emergency crews fighting 14 wildfires in South Wales. More than a dozen homes were gutted by fires in the West Midlands during the week, while temperatures reached 38.1°C on Thursday, the country's hottest day of the year.Firefighters made progress against another blaze in Germany's Hurtgen Forest, allowing about 2,000 residents evacuated from Gey to return on Saturday. By Sunday, officials reported no open flames and said crews had created a cleared cordon around the affected area to stop the fire spreading.Croatia was also dealing with the aftermath of a wildfire along its coastline that began overnight on Friday. At least one person died and dozens were injured, while around 1,200 residents and tourists were evacuated.Croatia's fire chief Slavko Tucakovic called it “one of the worst” blazes in the country's history.The EU's Copernicus climate monitoring service has confirmed that western Europe recorded its hottest June-to-July period on record. Authorities in the UK warned that although the heatwave was easing, drought conditions meant the risk of wildfires remained high.
Article Summary: Two wildfires that broke out minutes apart on the Greek island of Salamina on Sunday killed two people. About 500 people, including beachgoers, were evacuated by sea. The fires were part of a wider outbreak across Europe over the weekend, with crews also battling major blazes in Belgium, France, Germany and Croatia.

Article Title: Lakshmi Mittal's Ukraine steel plant hit by Russian missile; 2 killed
Article Text:
MittalArcelor plant hit in Russian strikes

Russian attacks on Ukraine on Sunday struck a site at ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, the country’s largest steel producer owned by Indian billionaire Lakshmi Mittal , killing two people and injuring over 10 workers and contractors, the company told Kyiv Post.The missile strike hit the ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih mining and metallurgical plant in the central city of Kryvyi Rih on August 16, forcing the company to partially suspend operations.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Russian attack on Kryvyi Rih killed two people and wounded 14 others. He also reported one death in the northeastern city of Sumy.ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, the Ukrainian unit of the world’s second-largest steelmaker, confirmed that one of its sites was hit in the missile attack.The strikes also caused casualties and damage elsewhere in Ukraine. In the southern Zaporizhzhia region, a man and a woman were killed after their home was hit, according to Ivan Fedorov, head of the regional military administration.In Kyiv, Russian attacks sparked several fires and injured six people. A major fire broke out at one of the capital’s largest book markets near the Pochaina metro station, destroying rows of closely packed kiosks and sending thick plumes of black smoke into the sky.“Wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said.Russia’s defence ministry said its forces had targeted a metallurgical plant in Kryvyi Rih as well as several military-industrial facilities in Kyiv, including a site involved in manufacturing Ukraine’s Flamingo missiles.The Ukrainian-made long-range missiles have become increasingly important to Kyiv’s attacks on Russian territory. Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Ukraine had used the weapons to strike a rocket research and production centre in Samara, about 900 km (560 miles) from the Ukrainian border.The escalating conflict between the two neighbouring countries saw Ukraine launch one of its largest aerial attacks on Russia, killing at least six people on Sunday.Ukraine unleashed hundreds of drones across Russia, with Kyiv stepping up long-range strikes on military and energy facilities as well as major commercial sites.Russia’s defence ministry said it had destroyed 822 Ukrainian drones overnight, including hundreds headed towards Moscow. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said around 600 drones were detected near the capital.An 83-year-old man was killed after a Ukrainian drone struck a home in the Moscow region, while another attack sparked a fire at a Wildberries warehouse in Podolsk.Ukraine also came under heavy Russian attack, with drone strikes destroying homes and setting fire to Kyiv’s landmark book market.
Article Summary: ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, the Ukrainian unit of the world’s second-largest steelmaker, confirmed that one of its sites was hit in the missile attack. In Kyiv, Russian attacks sparked several fires and injured six people. Ukraine also came under heavy Russian attack, with drone strikes destroying homes.

Article Title: Tropical Storm Lala moves away from Hawaii, leaves trail of damage and lakhs without power
Article Text:
Damage along a roadway on the eastern edge of Hawaii's Big Island from Hurricane Lala (AP photo)

Damage across the islands

Lakhs without power

Major impact without landfall

Tropical Storm Lala began moving away from Hawaii on Sunday after battering the islands with heavy rain and powerful winds, leaving at least 100 homes damaged or swept away and nearly 1,84,000 customers without power. Lala formed as a tropical storm on August 13 and strengthened into a Category 1 hurricane as it approached the Big Island on Saturday, before weakening again as it moved westward.The storm brought torrential rain, flash flooding, landslides and hurricane-force wind gusts across Hawaii. More than 30 inches of rain fell in parts of the Big Island, while gusts at higher elevations topped 161 kph. Despite the scale of the damage, Lala never made landfall, with its eyewall passing close to the southern coast of the Big Island.Hawaii governor Josh Green said at least 100 homes were damaged or swept away on the Big Island. No deaths have been confirmed in connection with the homes that were washed away, although officials were investigating two other deaths to determine whether they were storm-related.Rescue teams were sent to the coastal communities of Naalehu and Waiohinu after floodwaters swept through the area. Green said an elderly woman was rescued from a tree after her home was washed away.Flooding also damaged roads and small bridges. A section of highway near Pahala collapsed after floodwaters surged across it, leaving up to 2,500 residents isolated. Green warned that the Big Island was likely to have suffered numerous landslides.More than 30 inches of rain fell in parts of the Big Island, while higher elevations recorded up to 89 cm. In Honolulu, the fire department received more than 600 weather-related calls by Sunday afternoon, including 147 reports of fallen trees. Roofs were blown off and power lines were brought down in several areas.More than 190 flights were postponed and 52 were cancelled, although airports across the state remained open.Around 184,000 homes and businesses were still without electricity across Hawaii as Lala moved west. Nearly 70% of customers on the Big Island had lost power.At least three hospitals were operating on generators, while fallen trees and damaged roads were slowing repair and emergency work. Officials said some communities remained difficult to reach because of washed-out roads and bridges.Honolulu also saw widespread disruption, with fallen trees, damaged infrastructure and flooded roads reported across the city.Tropical storm warnings remained in effect for several islands, with forecasters warning that heavy rain could continue to trigger flash floods and mudslides even as Lala moved away.Lala strengthened into a Category 1 hurricane on Saturday before weakening to a tropical storm. It made its closest approach to the Big Island at around 5 p.m. local time, with its eyewall passing roughly 30 miles offshore.The storm therefore did not make landfall, but its powerful winds and rain still battered the islands. Wind gusts reached more than 161 kph at the summit of Mauna Kea, while powerful waves hit the Big Island coast.The National Hurricane Center said Lala's effects were expected to move out of the Hawaiian Islands by Monday morning. However, the threat from flooding and mudslides remained as rainbands continued to pass over the islands.Forecasters also said Lala could strengthen again after moving farther west of Hawaii, potentially becoming a hurricane again by Tuesday or Wednesday.
Article Summary: More than 30 inches of rain fell in parts of the Big Island, while gusts at higher elevations topped 161 kph. More than 190 flights were postponed and 52 were cancelled, although airports across the state remained open. No deaths have been confirmed in connection with the homes that were washed away, although officials are investigating two other deaths.

Article Title: "The painful Erika white-knighting": Candace Owens accuses Andrew Wilson of wasting viewers’ time in explosive Tyler Robinson debate
Article Text:
Candace Owens (Image via Getty)

Candace Owens highlights Tyler Robinson charges in viral debate moment

Andrew Wilson debate clip sparks wider Charlie Kirk case discussion

Candace Owens has turned one tense exchange from her debate with Andrew Wilson into a fresh flashpoint online. During their heated discussion surrounding the Charlie Kirk killing and the case against Tyler Robinson, Owens challenged Wilson to identify a charge filed against Robinson. The moment quickly spread across social media, with Owens later arguing that Wilson had spent too much time defending Erika Kirk instead of engaging with the legal details she wanted to debate.The exchange became significant because the criminal case against Robinson is built around specific charges, with aggravated murder at the center. Prosecutors have also brought additional counts involving firearm discharge, obstruction of justice, witness tampering and a violent offense committed in the presence of a child.Owens appeared to believe Wilson should have been prepared to discuss those details before entering a debate focused heavily on the circumstances surrounding Kirk's death and the prosecution of Robinson.After the debate, she explained her frustration in a post:“The craziest part is this really wasn’t supposed to be a gotcha. Hence me asking which “one”.I felt he severely wasted viewers time with the painful Erika white-knighting, and I actually wanted to debate him on the substance of Utah’s law regarding the aggravating factor.Then I realized ‘oh wait... wow. This man literally does not even know what Tyler Robinson was charged with’.And this is who TPUSA brought in to debate-train their students.”That statement shifts the focus away from simply who performed better in the debate. Owens is framing the exchange as a question of preparation and knowledge, particularly because the legal issue surrounding aggravating factors could influence whether prosecutors can pursue the death penalty.Robinson's defense has recently argued that the alleged shooting does not satisfy the required aggravating circumstances for capital punishment. Prosecutors, however, have argued that firing from a rooftop toward a crowded area and preparing additional ammunition support their position. A judge is expected to consider whether the case can proceed as a capital matter.The viral moment gained even more traction after the account Unfuck America Tour reposted the exchange with its own framing:“🚨 THIS is the moment that will be remembered from the entire debate.Andrew Wilson was asked to name ONE charge against Tyler Robinson.He couldn’t....”The clip has since become a talking point among viewers judging the Owens-Wilson confrontation. Some see it as a damaging preparation failure for Wilson, while others argue that naming a criminal charge during a heated debate is only one part of assessing a much larger argument.That distinction matters. The viral exchange does not by itself establish who was right about the broader claims discussed during the debate. It does, however, explain why the moment has resonated online.The Robinson case remains before the Utah courts, and he has not yet entered a plea. Prosecutors continue to pursue the case while his defense challenges the state's arguments, meaning the legal process will ultimately determine the facts and charges that matter in court, rather than a viral debate clip.
Article Summary: Candace Owens challenged Andrew Wilson to name a charge in the Tyler Robinson case. Owens argued that Wilson had spent too much time defending Erika Kirk instead of engaging with the legal details she wanted to debate. The viral clip has since become a talking point among viewers judging the Owens-Wilson confrontation.

Article Title: Did Suki Mellow and Kanel Joseph break up? Streamer’s emotional confession sparks fresh relationship rumors
Article Text:
Suki Mellow opens up about Kanel Joseph relationship

Kanel Joseph breakup rumors spread after Suki Mellow comments

Suki Mellow and Kanel Joseph’s relationship has become a talking point among fans after the Twitch streamer opened up about where things stand between them. Following their appearance together at Streamer Prom, Suki spoke warmly about Kanel while also admitting that they may be in different places in life. Her comments did not confirm a breakup, but the emotional tone has left viewers wondering whether the pair have quietly gone their separate ways.During a recent stream, Suki addressed Kanel with a mix of affection, regret and understanding. Rather than criticizing him, she described him as someone she deeply respects and suggested that she hopes they can spend time together again under different circumstances.She said:"He’s great, though. He’s a great person, and he is wonderful, and I’m so happy I met him. And I hope that we can hang out again. And I hope that the next time that we hang out, like, I can be a better version of myself, you know? I can maybe be a version of myself that, like, can manage my emotions."That choice of words immediately caught attention. Suki did not accuse Kanel of doing anything wrong. Instead, she looked inward and acknowledged that emotions may have played a role in how their situation developed.She also appeared to recognize that a relationship can become complicated when two people have different schedules, ambitions and expectations. Kanel, she explained, has significant responsibilities outside streaming, including running his business.Suki added:"You have to understand that people have priorities, and that those priorities don’t make you less valuable. They just mean that you’re in two different parts of, like, your life, maybe wanting different things. And yeah. Yeah. And, like, and also, like, he is so busy. Like, I genuinely, like, I genuinely just want to see him do good. He’s so busy. I feel so bad for him, you know? He’s always… he’s got so much on his plate. Like, you guys don’t get it. He, like, literally manages, like, a whole ****** business."Fans quickly began interpreting Suki’s comments as evidence that the relationship had ended. Several viewers on X shared theories about what may have happened, although those reactions remain speculation rather than confirmation from either streamer.The discussion became even more complicated because Suki and Kanel’s public interactions have sometimes taken place in a content-driven environment. Their appearance at Streamer Prom, in particular, led viewers to debate whether their connection was genuine, part of online content, or something that developed naturally beyond the cameras.Suki later appeared to offer a simpler answer when Jasontheween asked her about Kanel during a "Last to Leave" challenge. She told Jason:"Yeah, me too. I’m good. I’m good with Kanel. Kanel is a sweet guy."That response suggests there is no public feud between the two. Still, her more emotional comments have left plenty of room for interpretation.For now, there is no clear confirmation that Suki Mellow and Kanel Joseph have officially broken up. What is clear is that Suki continues to speak positively about Kanel and appears to want the best for him. Until either streamer directly defines their relationship, breakup claims remain fan speculation rather than an established fact.
Article Summary: Suki Mellow and Kanel Joseph's relationship has become a talking point among fans after the Twitch streamer opened up about where things stand between them. Her comments did not confirm a breakup, but the emotional tone has left viewers wondering whether the pair have quietly gone their separate ways.

Article Title: Zelenskyy seeks 10% of US stockpile to 'destroy all Russians’ missiles’: Report
Article Text:
Zelensky urged the US to sell Ukraine 5-10% of its Patriot interceptor stockpile to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks

Zelensky describes daily efforts to secure missiles

Uncertainty over Ukraine's Patriot production

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you support the idea of the US providing more Patriot missiles to Ukraine? Yes, absolutely No, they should focus on diplomacy 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Zelensky seeks greater US role in peace talks

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has urged the United States to sell Ukraine more Patriot interceptor missiles, saying even 5% of the US stockpile would help Kyiv survive the winter, while 10% could allow it to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.Zelensky made the comments in an interview with CNN as Ukraine faces a sharp increase in Russian ballistic missile attacks and a severe shortage of Patriot interceptors.“This year we have two and a half times less interceptors than we had in 2025,” he said. “Russia has two times more ballistic missiles per month than they had before.”“If they can sell us 10%, we will destroy all the Russians’ ballistic missiles. I have 1%.”Zelensky said Russia's intensified attacks had placed further pressure on Ukraine's air defences, particularly around Kyiv. The United Nations has said July was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022.“Each night you have attacks, and four or five times per month we have massive attacks … terrible nights. Very heroic, very resilient people really. But they (are) tired.”Zelensky said securing additional interceptors had become a daily priority, involving direct appeals to the US and negotiations with other allies.“This is what I live each day: from 1% to 5%. I have some months, and million phone calls … I try to exchange something to missiles … I do some things which I can’t even share. It doesn’t mean that it’s outside of the law. But I can’t speak about it.”He said the global supply of Patriot missiles had been strained by the US war with Iran, during which American and Gulf forces used dozens of interceptors against Iranian missile and drone attacks.The shortage has left Ukraine facing growing difficulty in defending its cities against Russian missile strikes.Zelensky also said uncertainty remained over a proposal for Ukraine to manufacture Patriot interceptor missiles under a US licence.US President Donald Trump had said during the Nato summit in Ankara that he would allow Ukraine to obtain a licence to manufacture the systems. However, Trump later expressed uncertainty about the proposal.Patriot system manufacturers have since sent officials to Kyiv to discuss potential production, but Zelensky said no agreement had yet been reached.“I hope that I will get it,” Zelensky said. “I don’t have now 5% and I don’t have such an acceptance. And this is for me is a big challenge, one of the biggest I had from the very beginning of this war.”Zelensky said he had been appealing directly to the White House through calls and messages, as well as through Ukraine's allies, to secure additional Patriot support.Zelensky also said Ukraine had presented new proposals for the US-led peace process, while calling for greater American involvement.“We need more involvement of the American side to the peace plan. I’m thankful to the team of President Trump that they want to continue. (Russian President Vladimir) Putin doesn’t want to stop this war now and (there’s) not enough pressure on him now.”He rejected the possibility of Ukraine surrendering the remaining territory in the Donbass sought by Russian President Vladimir Putin, saying security guarantees remained essential to prevent another invasion.“Russia begins to speak about this war, and they speak about territory. The key question is why he will not come again with 1 or 2 additional million soldiers after a big pause. Why he will not come again to occupy us?”Zelensky also backed Western assessments that Putin could eventually seek to escalate the conflict with Nato, including by targeting the Baltic states.“He doesn’t know how to end this war without big occupation or big victory for his society. It’s more simple to find some smaller country … for him, it will not be important if this country is in Nato or not in Nato. He wants quick victory, 100% sure that he will win, occupy or destroy or control.”
Article Summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has urged the United States to sell Ukraine more Patriot interceptor missiles. He said even 5% of the US stockpile would help Kyiv survive the winter, while 10% could allow it to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks. Zelenski said securing additional interceptors had become a daily priority.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Rabindranath Tagore: "Everything comes to us that belongs to us if we…" - a lesson on preparation, patience and being ready when opportunity arrives
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Rabindranath Tagore (Image: Wikipedia)

Quote of the day by Rabindranath Tagore

"Everything comes to us that belongs to us if we create the capacity to receive it"

Understand the meaning of Rabindranath Tagore's quote

What "capacity to receive" actually means

Why simply wanting something is rarely enough on its own

Why preparation changes what someone is even able to notice

Why growth so often happens quietly, long before any reward arrives

Why this idea is not really a promise that everything works out

How this idea extends into relationships as well

Other memorable quotes by Rabindranath Tagore

"You can't cross the sea merely by standing and staring at the water."

"Faith is the bird that feels the light when the dawn is still dark."

"Let your life lightly dance on the edges of Time like dew on the tip of a leaf."

"Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high."

Why Rabindranath Tagore's quote remains relevant
Article Summary: "Everything comes to us that belongs to us if we create the capacity to receive it" "Faith is the bird that feels the light when the dawn is still dark" "Let your life lightly dance on the edges of Time like dew on the tip of a leaf" "Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high"

Article Title: Indian-origin teen charged with murdering mother, brother in US after ‘kill family’ searches
Article Text:
Indian-origin teenager charged with double murder of mother, brother in Massachusetts.

A 17-year-old Indian-origin teenager has been charged with allegedly murdering his mother and younger brother at their home in Acton, Massachusetts, authorities said.The teen has been charged with two counts of murder, two counts each of assault and battery on a household or family member and assault and battery, along with charges of using a vehicle without authority and stealing a motor vehicle.The 17-year old is accused of fatally assaulting his mother, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and his 14-year-old brother, Siddharth Aravind, inside their Martha Lane home on Tuesday before fleeing in his mother's car.Middlesex district attorney Marian Ryan and acton police chief Douglas Sturniolo said police received a call from teen's father shortly after 6.37 pm on August 11 after he was unable to contact his family. A tutor expected at the house had also been unable to reach anyone.The father had last spoken to Sudha early Tuesday morning before leaving for work, while Siddharth was last seen around noon, authorities said.Police who arrived at the house found both victims dead. Siddharth was found on the first floor and Sudha in the finished basement. Both victims were found with “obvious trauma”, but the chief medical examiner has yet to release information on the exact cause and manner of death.The type of weapon used in the killings is also still under investigation.The accused was not at the house when police arrived and was believed to have fled in his mother's vehicle. Investigators issued an alert for him as they searched for the teenager.He was found early Wednesday in the vehicle in a parking lot in Wayland, Massachusetts, after local police responded to an unrelated alarm. He was taken into custody without incident.The Middlesex county district attorney's office said investigators found that Arjun had recently displayed concerning behaviour."The subsequent investigation indicates that Arjun had recently been demonstrating concerning behaviour, including using the internet and ChatGPT to make searches for theoretical ideas or fantasies regarding killing his family,” the statement said.Arjun was expected to be arraigned in Lowell juvenile court on Wednesday. However, the juvenile court does not have jurisdiction over murder charges. He will therefore face arraignment on the murder and related assault charges in Concord district court later.
Article Summary: Indian-origin teenager charged with double murder of mother, brother in Massachusetts. The 17-year-old is accused of fatally assaulting his mother, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and his brother, Siddharth Aravind, 14. The teen has been charged with two counts of murder, two counts each of assault and battery.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Melinda French Gates: "When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually…" - a lesson on stepping outside your comfort zone
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Melinda French Gates

Quote of the day by Melinda French Gates

"When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that"

Where this quote actually comes from

What the quote is actually saying

Why discomfort can genuinely be a sign of progress

Why stepping outside a comfort zone actually matters

Why failure is genuinely part of growth

Why real confidence tends to develop through experience, not before it

Why this idea applies directly to professional life

A note on Melinda French Gates

Other famous quotes by Melinda French Gates

"That is why we women have to lift each other up, not to replace men at the top of the hierarchy, but to become partners with men in ending hierarchy."

"I've never held the view that women are better than men, or that the best way to improve the world is for women to gain more power than men."

"Embrace change. Don't be afraid of it."

"I am simply not willing to accept that my granddaughters could grow up with less freedom than I did."

Why this quote continues to inspire people

Growth rarely feels comfortable while it is actually happening. Learning something new, taking on more responsibility, or simply stepping into an unfamiliar situation tends to bring real uncertainty along with it. Melinda French Gates put a name to that discomfort directly. "When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that," she said. Rather than treating discomfort as an automatic warning sign, her point is that it often means something else entirely, that an old habit or a familiar limit is genuinely being challenged, and that the challenge itself is usually exactly where real growth actually happens. Her words encourage people to look at discomfort with greater curiosity, recognising that difficult moments can sometimes signal progress rather than failure or a reason to retreat. That practice of consciously reframing discomfort as evidence of growth, rather than a signal to retreat, reflects a deliberate mental habit French Gates has clearly cultivated over years of navigating unfamiliar and often high-pressure situations herself.French Gates said this in a Forbes interview with Marianne Schnall, published in April 2025, while discussing her memoir The Next Day, released the same year. She went further in the same conversation, describing exactly how she talks herself through discomfort in real time. "I'll literally coach myself in my head," she said. "'Okay, this is hard, but I must be growing here. It's going to be okay.' And then on the other side, you actually become far more resilient. " She added a piece of broader advice in the same interview too, "Embrace change. Don't be afraid of it... just know you've got a lot of tools inside of you." For French Gates, that mindset reflects the value of recognising difficult moments as opportunities to adapt, learn and develop greater confidence.Staying inside a comfort zone usually means staying inside the familiar, where there is less uncertainty and fewer situations that genuinely test existing ability. Growth tends to happen specifically once someone runs into something unfamiliar instead, a new responsibility that feels overwhelming, a moment of speaking up that feels intimidating, a new skill that feels frustrating at first. None of that discomfort is pleasant in the moment. It is often exactly what gradually expands what a person is actually capable of. This is why people who consistently seek out unfamiliar challenges tend to develop broader skill sets over time, while those who remain within familiar routines, however comfortable, often find their growth quietly stalling without ever fully realising it.Comfort usually comes from familiarity. When something feels uncomfortable, it often simply means someone has not fully mastered it yet, and that unfamiliarity is precisely what creates room to actually learn. A first attempt at something new is rarely smooth. Repeated effort is usually what eventually turns that uncertainty into real confidence, which is really how most skills get built in the first place.Comfort zones are not inherently a problem. They provide genuine stability and give people room to recover between challenges. The real issue starts once fear of discomfort stops someone trying anything new at all. Taking calculated steps beyond a familiar routine tends to expose people to new ideas and real opportunity, and over time, the boundaries of what actually feels comfortable start expanding on their own.Growth does not only happen through success. A mistake can reveal exactly where a real weakness sits. A difficult conversation can improve how someone communicates going forward. A rejected opportunity can push someone to prepare more thoroughly next time. Rather than treating every setback as proof of inadequacy, it can just as easily become useful information that helps someone actually improve.Confidence is not always something someone has to already possess before taking action. More often, it develops precisely because they took the action despite feeling genuinely uncertain about it. Each difficult experience becomes real evidence that a person can actually handle a challenge, and that evidence is what slowly builds resilience and self-belief over time.Career growth regularly requires people to take on responsibilities they have never handled before. A promotion might suddenly demand real leadership skill. A new job might involve completely unfamiliar systems. Avoiding those moments can feel comfortable in the short term, but it tends to limit development considerably further down the line, while embracing a reasonable challenge tends to open the door to real professional growth instead.Melinda French Gates is an American philanthropist, author and advocate who has worked extensively on global health, gender equality and women's economic empowerment. She co-founded the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, stepped away from it in 2024, and went on to lead Pivotal Ventures, an investment and incubation organisation she founded to advance social progress. Her 2019 book The Moment of Lift: How Empowering Women Changes the World explored many of these same themes at length.French Gates' words offer a genuinely simple way to rethink the moments that actually make people uncomfortable. Not every difficult experience is really a setback. Sometimes discomfort is exactly the evidence that someone is learning, adapting and becoming capable of something they genuinely could not do before. "When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that" is really a reminder to approach unfamiliar experiences with curiosity rather than retreating from them immediately. Growth takes real patience, involves real mistakes, and often just requires the courage to stay in an uncomfortable situation long enough to actually learn something from it.
Article Summary: "When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that" Melinda French Gates said this in a Forbes interview with Marianne Schnall, published in April 2025, while discussing her memoir The Next Day. French Gates has clearly cultivated over years of navigating unfamiliar and often high-pressure situations herself.

Article Title: Where is Bashar al-Assad? Ousted Syrian dictator sentenced to death in absentia
Article Text:
Synrian Ex-president Bashar Assad (2019 photo)

where is Bashar al-Assad now, and can Syria ever bring him back to face the punishment handed down by its court?

Assad remains in Russia after fleeing Syria

Where exactly in Moscow is Assad living?

Bashar Assad, left, and Russian President Vladimir Putin shake hands during their meeting in Moscow, Russia.

Russia has kept Assad away from public life

Why Syria sentenced Assad to death

Syria sentences absent Bashar al-Assad to death over killings and torture (Image: Reuters)

Verdict welcomed by Assad's victims

Can Syria actually bring Assad back?

From Syria's president to a secluded exile

Bashar al-Assad inherited his presidency from his father

A Syrian criminal court in Damascus has sentenced ousted president Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia after finding him guilty of killings, torture, arbitrary arrests and crimes against humanity committed during the country's nearly 14-year civil war. The verdict, delivered on Tuesday, August 11, marks the first conviction against Assad by Syria's transitional authorities since his regime collapsed in December 2024. But while the court has pronounced a death sentence, the former Syrian ruler remains far beyond the reach of the authorities who now control Damascus.Assad is currently in Russia, where he and his family were granted asylum after fleeing Syria when rebel forces captured Damascus in December 2024. His precise location inside Russia has not been publicly confirmed. However, reporting over the past year has placed the former dictator in Moscow, with sources previously indicating that his family was likely living in the heavily guarded Rublyovka area, an affluent district on the western outskirts of the Russian capital.The death sentence therefore raises a central question:The most recent credible reports continue to place Assad in Moscow.Reuters reported after Tuesday's verdict that Assad "is currently in Russia", where he and his family received asylum on humanitarian grounds. His brother Maher al-Assad, who also received a death sentence in absentia, is likewise believed to be in Russia.Assad's escape from Syria came on December 8, 2024, when rebel forces led by Ahmed al-Sharaa swept into Damascus after a lightning offensive that lasted less than two weeks. The advance brought down the Assad government and ended more than five decades of rule by the Assad family.At the time, Assad's whereabouts were initially unknown. Russia's foreign ministry said he had resigned and left Syria, while reports suggested he had travelled from the coastal region before being flown to Russia. Russian state media subsequently reported that Assad and his family had arrived in Moscow and had been granted asylum.In a statement issued after his escape, Assad disputed accounts that he had planned his departure in advance. He said he had remained in Damascus until the final hours and later moved to a Russian military base in Latakia as the security situation deteriorated."First, my departure from Syria was neither planned nor did it occur during the final hours of the battles, as some have claimed," Assad said in the statement."On the contrary, I remained in Damascus, carrying out my duties until the early hours of Sunday, December 8, 2024," he added.According to Assad's account, he travelled to the Russian Khmeimim airbase in Latakia after opposition forces entered Damascus and intended to continue overseeing military operations. He said the situation at the base then became untenable and Moscow asked its command to arrange his evacuation."With no viable means of leaving the base, Moscow requested that the base's command arrange an immediate evacuation to Russia on the evening of Sunday 8 December," the statement said.Independent reporting has also described Assad's departure as a Russian-assisted evacuation. The Guardian reported in December 2025 that Assad and his sons were taken under Russian military escort to Khmeimim before being flown out of Syria.This is where the trail becomes less certain. There is no publicly verified address for Assad in Moscow, and he has rarely, if ever, been seen publicly since arriving in Russia. A detailed Guardian investigation published in December 2025, based on sources in Russia and Syria, a family friend and leaked data, reported that the Assad family was likely living in Rublyovka, a prestigious gated area associated with Russia's political and business elite.The report described the family's life in Moscow as secluded and closely controlled. A family friend said Assad had little contact with the outside world and remained in touch with only a small number of people who had served around his presidential palace."It's a very quiet life," said the family friend. "He has very little, if any, contact with the outside world. He's only in touch with a couple of people who were in his palace, like Mansour Azzam [former Syrian minister of presidency affairs] and Yassar Ibrahim [Assad's top economic crony]."The same investigation said Assad was studying Russian and revisiting his training in ophthalmology. Before entering politics, Assad had trained as an ophthalmologist in London and had originally intended to pursue a medical career before the death of his elder brother Basil changed the succession plans of the Assad family."He’s studying Russian and brushing up on his ophthalmology again," a family friend told the Guardian. "It’s a passion of his, he obviously doesn’t need the money. Even before the war in Syria began, he used to regularly practice his ophthalmology in Damascus."However, the Rublyovka location should be treated as a reported possibility rather than a confirmed current address. What is firmly established is that Assad remains in Russia and has been kept away from public political life.Moscow's decision to shelter Assad has been one of the biggest obstacles to attempts by Syria's new authorities to bring the former president before a court.Russia granted Assad and his family asylum on humanitarian grounds after the fall of his government. Since then, reports have indicated that the Kremlin has placed restrictions on his public activities.In a November 2025 interview cited by the Guardian, Russia's ambassador to Iraq, Elbrus Kutrashev, said Assad was safe in Russia but could not engage in political or media activity."Assad may live here but cannot engage in political activities … He has no right to engage in any media or political activity. Have you heard anything from him? You haven’t, because he is not allowed to – but he is safe and alive," Kutrashev said.The restrictions have contributed to the mystery surrounding Assad's life in exile. Unlike other deposed leaders who have appeared publicly after leaving office, Assad has remained largely invisible.His children, however, have had a somewhat more visible life in Moscow. The Guardian reported that Assad's daughter Zein attended the prestigious Moscow State Institute of International Relations, known as MGIMO, and graduated in June 2025. Other family members were also seen at the ceremony, although they kept a low profile.The family has also reportedly travelled to the United Arab Emirates, a destination with which it had longstanding connections. But reports said the family initially hoped to relocate there permanently and later concluded that such a move would be difficult because of the political implications of hosting Assad.The Damascus court's verdict is the first Syrian conviction against Assad himself. The court found him guilty of offences including premeditated and intentional murder, torture, arbitrary arrest and crimes against humanity. His younger brother Maher was handed the same sentence in absentia.Maher commanded Syria's elite Fourth Armoured Division and was one of the most powerful military figures under Assad. The division was repeatedly accused by opposition activists and rights groups of involvement in crackdowns, killings and torture during the conflict.Assad's cousin Atef Najib, the former head of political security in Deraa province, was also sentenced to death. Unlike Assad and Maher, Najib was in Syrian custody and appeared in court wearing a prison uniform.Najib's role is particularly important because Deraa is widely regarded as the birthplace of the 2011 uprising against Assad. The unrest began after security forces detained and allegedly tortured teenagers who had written anti-government graffiti on a school wall.The crackdown that followed helped turn local protests into nationwide demonstrations. The government's violent response contributed to the escalation into an armed conflict that eventually drew in regional and global powers.The court also sentenced several other former military and security officials to death in absentia, including former defence minister Fahd al-Freij and former military intelligence chief in Deraa Louay al-Ali.The ruling was met with celebrations in parts of Syria, particularly in areas that suffered heavily under Assad's security forces.Crowds gathered outside the courthouse in Damascus, chanting and waving Syrian flags. In Deraa, families of people killed or detained during the early years of the uprising gathered with photographs of their relatives.For many victims, the verdict carried significance beyond the punishment itself. It was an official acknowledgement by Syria's new authorities of crimes committed during the Assad era.Noha al-Masri, a prosecutor involved in the case, lost her brother during the crackdown in Deraa in 2011."We have been waiting for 15 years to reclaim even a small part of our rights, for all those who have spilled our blood, committed crimes, violated our rights, killed, and tortured us," Masri told the BBC."Our demand is that this not be the end of the trials... In the new Syria, there will be no impunity from this day forward."Reuters reported that the trial process lasted nearly four months and was presented by Syria's new authorities as part of a wider effort to pursue transitional justice after the fall of Assad.But the verdict has also drawn criticism from human rights groups over the fairness of the proceedings. The Associated Press reported that rights organisations raised concerns about whether the trials were rushed and whether defendants received adequate legal protections. Human Rights Watch also criticised the use of the death penalty, saying accountability requires a justice system capable of guaranteeing fair trials.For now, the answer appears to be no. The death sentence has no immediate practical effect on Assad because he is outside Syrian territory and under Russian protection. Syria would need Russia to surrender him or otherwise allow him to be transferred to Syrian custody.Anwar al-Bunni, head of the Syrian Centre for Legal Studies and Research, argued that the death sentence itself could make extradition harder."There is a huge problem, which is that no one will hand over a criminal to a country that issues a death sentence. This will cut off the road to Assad, and many other criminals, being handed over to Syria," Bunni told Reuters."This is performative justice, not transitional justice," he said.Syria's new authorities have previously sought accountability for Assad and senior figures from his government. The issue has also been part of the complicated relationship between Damascus and Moscow. Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa travelled to Moscow in October 2025 for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, with Assad's extradition among the issues surrounding the relationship.Assad also faces legal action outside Syria. France has issued an arrest warrant against him over allegations connected to the bombing of a press centre in Homs in 2012, according to Reuters.Assad inherited the presidency in 2000 after the death of his father, Hafez al-Assad, who had ruled Syria for nearly three decades. Bashar initially presented himself as a modernising leader, but his rule became increasingly associated with political repression and the security apparatus.The defining event of his presidency was the 2011 uprising. What began as protests demanding political change developed into a devastating civil war involving the Syrian government, opposition groups, extremist organisations and foreign powers. Russia intervened militarily in support of Assad in 2015, helping his forces regain territory and eventually reducing the opposition's hold over much of the country.For years, Assad appeared to have survived the war. Then, in late 2024, the balance changed with extraordinary speed.Forces led by Ahmed al-Sharaa launched an offensive from northern Syria and advanced rapidly towards Damascus. On December 8, the capital fell and the Assad government collapsed.The man who had ruled Syria for more than two decades disappeared from the country and resurfaced in Moscow.Nearly two years later, a Syrian court has sentenced him to death. Yet the most important fact remains unchanged: Bashar al-Assad is not in a Syrian prison. He is in Russia, living under the protection of the country that stood by his regime during the civil war.His exact whereabouts in Moscow remain undisclosed. Reports have pointed to the elite Rublyovka district, while other details of his life suggest a tightly controlled existence away from politics and public view.The Damascus verdict therefore closes one chapter of Assad's rule, but not the question of whether the former Syrian president will ever return to the country he ruled for 24 years.For now, the death sentence exists on paper in Damascus while Assad remains thousands of kilometres away in Russia.
Article Summary: Bashar al-Assad was sentenced to death in absentia by a Syrian court. He was found guilty of killings, torture, arbitrary arrests and crimes against humanity. Assad fled Syria when rebel forces captured Damascus in December 2024. He and his family were granted asylum in Russia, where they are believed to be living.

Article Title: ‘Very good’ ties with Kim: Trump orders 'substantial' cut in military drills with South Korea
Article Text:
Trump on Saturday shared a throwback photograph with Kim Jong Un, joking about their "unfriendly look" while reaffirming that the two get along well. (Image credit: Truth Social)

US-South Korea drills under scrutiny

Trump backs Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defence pact

US President Donald Trump has ordered the Pentagon to “substantially” reduce planned joint military exercises with South Korea, citing his “very good relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and Seoul’s refusal to join US efforts to denuclearise Iran.Trump said the military exercises, scheduled to begin this week, would send an inappropriate and hostile signal to North Korea, which he claimed had remained “unthreatening and respectful” during his presidency.In a post on social media, Trump said: "Based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un, of North Korea, I am not happy with the fact that the United States has, long ago, agreed to participate in Joint Military Exercises with South Korea. These exercises are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful."He added: "Therefore, and based on the fact that it is too late to cancel, I have instructed Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, to substantially reduce the Joint Military Exercises!"Trump also linked his decision to South Korea's position on Iran, saying he had recently asked the South Korean president whether Seoul wanted to join Washington's efforts to denuclearise Iran."While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, "No thanks!" Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP"The 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises are scheduled to involve around 18,000 South Korean troops and are designed to strengthen the allies' readiness against potential threats from North Korea, according to AP.Trump said cancelling the exercises altogether was no longer possible because preparations were already underway, but ordered Hegseth to reduce their scale.The exercises are intended to test the allies' ability to conduct complex joint operations. The US military has said they include live-fire exercises, precision targeting, manoeuvres, a wet-gap crossing and the distribution of pre-positioned military equipment.The drills have long been a source of tension with Pyongyang. North Korea condemned the exercises on Friday as a “rehearsal for an aggressive war” and threatened unspecified countermeasures against the US and South Korea.The latest development also comes after North Korea resumed ballistic missile testing. Earlier this month, South Korea, the US and Japan detected the launch of a short-range ballistic missile by Pyongyang, its first such test since late June.Trump's comments signal a renewed focus on his personal relationship with Kim as a factor in Washington's approach to military exercises on the Korean peninsula. Trump has repeatedly sought engagement with the North Korean leader during his presidency, while Washington and Seoul have continued to maintain their military alliance as a deterrent against Pyongyang.Separately, Trump welcomed a newly signed defence agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, describing it as a “big, bold” first step towards greater regional security cooperation.In a post on Truth Social, Trump said, “Very happy to see that Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan have recently, and finally, signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.”“It shows how the Middle East is coming together, and how Countries will finally be able to defend themselves in a more meaningful way,” he said.“This is a big, bold, and important first step — wow!” Trump added.The trilateral agreement was signed at a joint defence summit attended by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.The pact aims to deepen security and defence cooperation among the three countries. Pakistan's foreign ministry said the agreement is based on their historical ties, shared strategic interests and longstanding defence cooperation.It also includes a commitment that an armed attack against any one of the three countries would be regarded as an attack against all three.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump has ordered the Pentagon to “substantially” reduce planned joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump said the military exercises would send an inappropriate and hostile signal to North Korea. The 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises are scheduled to involve around 18,000 South Korean troops. The drills have long been a source of tension with Pyongyang.

Article Title: In 1905, Hawaii introduced mosquitofish to control mosquitoes; the tiny fish later became linked to declines of native damselflies and other threatened species
Article Text:
Hawaii introduced mosquitofish to control mosquitoes

Predation causes major declines in native Damselflies

Disrupting Hawaii's freshwater ecosystems

Difficulties in controlling the fish

Introduced to Hawaii in 1905 to control disease-carrying mosquitoes, the eastern mosquitofish (Gambusia affinis) has caused major declines in native aquatic insects, including several threatened species of Hawaiian damselflies. Conservation reports from the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) show that the small, non-native fish has had a serious impact on Hawaii's freshwater ecosystems because of its aggressive and flexible feeding habits. The fish was originally brought from the southeastern United States during a period of agricultural expansion. It was then widely released into streams, drainage ditches and taro fields. Instead of eating only mosquito larvae, however, mosquitofish began feeding on many types of native aquatic animals. This changed local food webs and reduced populations of native species.USFWS assessments of Hawaii's native damselflies (Megalagrion species) identify predation by introduced fish as one of the major causes of population decline. Before non-native fish were introduced, Hawaii had few native freshwater predators in high-elevation streams.As a result, many native aquatic insects evolved without defenses against fast-moving fish. When mosquitofish spread into lower- and middle-elevation streams, they began feeding on young Hawaiian damselflies, known as naiads. These young insects live in calm pools and along the edges of streams. The USFWS Ecological Risk Screening Summary for Eastern Mosquitofish describes Gambusia affinis as a species with high ecological risk. The fish reproduces quickly, can survive in different water temperatures and tolerates low levels of oxygen. Native species such as the crimson Hawaiian damselfly (Megalagrion xanthe) and the flying-earlobe Hawaiian damselfly (Megalagrion nigrohamatum) have disappeared from large parts of their former ranges on Oahu, Molokai, Maui and Hawaii Island in areas where mosquitofish are found.The effects of mosquitofish extend beyond damselflies. The fish also compete with native stream fish, including Hawaii's endemic freshwater gobies, commonly called o'opu, for the small aquatic animals they both depend on for food. Mosquitofish also eat native freshwater crustaceans, including endemic shrimp known as o'pae kala'ole. Their feeding can also affect algae on streambeds by removing organisms that normally help control plant growth. USFWS biologists point out that mosquitofish are especially difficult to manage because they do not depend only on mosquito larvae for food. When mosquito numbers fall, the fish can quickly switch to other small aquatic animals. This allows them to survive while continuing to reduce populations of native species. Their reproductive ability makes the problem even harder to control. Female mosquitofish give birth to live young instead of laying eggs. As a result, even one pregnant female introduced into an isolated stream pool can potentially establish a population within a short time.Removing established mosquitofish from Hawaii's streams is challenging because the islands have complex and connected waterways. Streams can connect with groundwater springs, mountain taro fields and coastal areas. This makes trapping or using chemicals difficult because control methods could also harm native species. Current conservation efforts by the USFWS and state wildlife agencies focus on protecting high-elevation streams where natural waterfalls can prevent invasive fish from moving upstream. Wildlife managers are also installing barriers designed to keep invasive fish out of protected habitats. In some areas, captive-bred Hawaiian damselflies are being released into safer headwater streams to rebuild populations. Federal environmental assessments also stress the importance of preventing people from moving mosquitofish into remote, high-elevation streams. More than a century after the fish was introduced to control mosquitoes, Hawaii's experience shows how a species brought in for one purpose can create much larger ecological problems. Protecting the remaining native aquatic species now depends on controlling the spread of mosquitofish and keeping vulnerable freshwater habitats free of invasive predators.
Article Summary: The eastern mosquitofish (Gambusia affinis) was introduced to Hawaii in 1905 to control disease-carrying mosquitoes. The small, non-native fish has had a serious impact on Hawaii's freshwater ecosystems because of its aggressive and flexible feeding habits. Mosquitofish are especially difficult to manage because they do not depend only on mosquito larvae for food.

Article Title: At 15, Lynne Cox broke the English Channel record for men and women; at 30, after an 11-year wait for permission, she swam through 38°F water from Alaska to the Soviet Union
Article Text:
Lynne Cox: The Swim That Lifted the Iron Curtain

A record-breaking swimmer with a peaceful mission

Swimming through freezing water and heavy fog

A historic welcome on Soviet soil

"She proved by her courage how close to each other our peoples live."

Fifteen years after setting a world record in the English Channel, 30-year-old American endurance swimmer Lynne Cox entered the 38°F (3.3°C) waters of the Bering Strait and completed a historic 2.7-mile swim from the United States to the Soviet Union. On 7 August 1987, Cox swam from Little Diomede Island in Alaska to Soviet-controlled Big Diomede Island. Her journey crossed the International Date Line and the heavily guarded border between the two Cold War superpowers. Records from the National Park Service (NPS) Shared Beringia Heritage Program document how the swim followed an 11-year effort by Cox to receive permission from Soviet leaders. Her arrival on Soviet territory became an important moment in US-Soviet relations. Soviet General Secretary Mikhail Gorbachev and US President Ronald Reagan later praised the achievement during their historic nuclear arms talks in Washington that year.Cox was born into a family of open-water swimmers. She learned to swim at a young age with her brother Dave, while her grandfather had also completed a swim across the Hudson River. At 15, Cox gained international attention by breaking the overall world record for the fastest English Channel crossing by a man or woman.Three years later, she became the first woman to swim across New Zealand's Cook Strait. The 13.5-mile crossing took her through rough waters known for strong currents and sharks. Cox first came up with the idea of swimming across the Bering Strait in 1976. She wanted the journey to become a symbol of peace and show that ordinary people could build connections despite political tensions between the United States and Soviet Union. However, Cold War tensions made the plan difficult. Fundraising was challenging, and requests for permission from Soviet officials went unanswered for more than a decade. By 1987, Cox had paid much of the cost through her own savings and family support. Alaska Airlines also provided her with a free flight. She traveled to Little Diomede Island even though she did not yet have official permission to cross the border. Just 30 hours before the planned swim, tensions increased when two large Soviet naval ships moved into the middle of the strait. US fighter jets were then sent overhead. Permission finally arrived from Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev only 24 hours before Cox was scheduled to enter the water.The approval also allowed local Inupiaq guides to accompany Cox in traditional skin boats. Their participation was significant because it was the first time in more than 40 years that residents of the islands were allowed to cross the maritime border to visit relatives on the other island. On the morning of 7 August 1987, Cox entered the freezing water in thick fog. The cold immediately placed enormous stress on her body. In interviews preserved by the National Park Service, Cox described the experience: "The cold was like a huge vampire pulling the heat from my body." She said her fingers became grey from the extreme cold. Cox had only a magnetic compass to help guide her through the fog. Strong currents threatened to push her off course. Eventually, a Soviet support boat appeared and helped guide her toward the shore.An English-speaking Soviet journalist on the boat told Cox that an official reception group was waiting farther along the coast. Although she was suffering from severe hypothermia, Cox decided to continue swimming along the shoreline. She later explained that she wanted to reach the people waiting for her rather than simply touch the rocks and finish the crossing without making a human connection. As she approached the landing area, local residents and Soviet border guards gathered along the shore. For many of those watching, the moment was especially meaningful because the border between the islands had been closed for decades.Cox completed the swim in two hours and five minutes. By the time she reached the shore, she was too weak to pull herself onto the rocks. Two Soviet military officers reached into the water and pulled her out. Cox later remembered the warmth of their hands and hearing them speak Russian. For her, the moment confirmed that the difficult journey had succeeded. A medical tent had been set up on the beach. Soviet doctor Dr. Rita Zakarova treated Cox for hypothermia using hot-water bottles, insulated sleeping bags and other warming methods. The swim then gained international attention.Later that year, during the December 1987 summit in Washington, D.C., where Reagan and Gorbachev signed the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty, the two leaders raised a toast to Cox.Gorbachev praised her achievement, saying:The crossing also contributed to greater cooperation between the two countries in the Bering Strait region. In 1990, US President George H.W. Bush and Gorbachev announced joint plans for international conservation efforts across the Bering Strait. These initiatives helped establish the foundation for what later became the NPS Shared Beringia Heritage Program. Cox went on to write several books about her swimming career. She continues to work as an author, educator and public speaker, focusing on subjects including risk management, endurance and teamwork. Her 1987 swim remains remembered not simply as an extraordinary feat of endurance, but as a rare moment when an athlete physically crossed one of the world's most heavily guarded Cold War borders and helped demonstrate the possibility of connection between two divided nations.
Article Summary: Lynne Cox completed a 2.7-mile swim from the United States to the Soviet Union in 1987. Her journey crossed the International Date Line and the heavily guarded border between the two Cold War superpowers. Her arrival on Soviet territory became an important moment in US-Soviet relations.

Article Title: 'They were Indian, so we didn’t count them': US cleaning business owner faces scrutiny over racial profiling
Article Text:
North Carolina cleaning business owner faces scrutiny after saying his team did not count Indian callers as potential leads/Image: Getty Images

A North Carolina cleaning business owner has come under scrutiny after saying he instructed his team not to count Indian callers as potential customers, raising concerns about possible discrimination based on ethnicity.Robert Nolen wrote on X that he teaches his staff to “profile every client” and said:“They were Indian so we didn't count them as a lead.”He also said his team had separated Indian callers and discussed changing prices to discourage them from using the business. In another post, he wrote: “We don’t want your business.”The Indian American Advocacy Council (IAAC) is reviewing Nolen's public statements and seeking accounts from Indian customers, applicants, workers and contractors who believe they were treated differently because of their ethnicity or national origin.IAAC said the statements could raise legal concerns if they describe the way Nolen's business actually treats customers. The group also cited Charlotte rules that prohibit businesses from indicating that services will be denied or that customers are unwelcome because of national origin or ethnicity.
