Article Summary: Robert Nolen wrote on X that he teaches his staff to ‘profile every client’ He also said his team had separated Indian callers and discussed changing prices to discourage them from using the business. In another post, he wrote: “We don’t want your business”

Article Title: In 1953, Emma Gatewood tried hiking the Appalachian Trail, got lost and was rescued; two years later, at 67, she walked all 2,190 miles alone and made history
Article Text:
In 1953, Emma Gatewood tried hiking the Appalachian Trail, got lost and was rescued

Grandma Gatewood's Walk

Overcoming a difficult early life

Grandma Gatewood's Walk

A simple approach to a huge journey

National Geographic

Her equipment included:

A wool blanket, plastic shower curtain, tin cup, canteen and small cooking pot.

A Swiss Army knife, raincoat, warm coat, spare clothes and a first-aid kit.

Simple food such as raisins, nuts, chicken bouillon cubes and canned Vienna sausages.

Canvas Keds shoes, going through seven pairs during the journey.

Reaching Mount Katahdin

"Because I wanted to."

When park rangers found 65-year-old Emma Gatewood lost and confused in Maine in 1953 after she broke her glasses on the Appalachian Trail, they advised her to give up and return home. Two years later, at age 67, Gatewood returned to the trail. She started at Mount Oglethorpe in Georgia, kept her plans secret from her adult children and walked all 2,190 miles alone. In 1955, she became the first woman to complete a solo thru-hike of the Appalachian Trail in a single season. Known to millions as Grandma Gatewood, she completed the journey in 146 days and changed the way people viewed long-distance hiking and physical endurance. Her story, preserved in historical archives including the Appalachian Mountain Club (AMC) Library & Archives and described in Ben Montgomery's 2014 book, is a story of survival, strength and independence.Emma Rowena Caldwell was born on 25 October 1887 on a farm in Gallia County, Ohio. She grew up doing hard physical work with her 14 siblings in a small log cabin. Her father, Hugh Caldwell, was a Civil War veteran who had lost a leg. He also struggled with alcoholism and gambling. At 19, Emma married 26-year-old farmer Perry Clayton Gatewood. The marriage began decades of severe hardship. In, Montgomery, who is Gatewood's great-great-grandnephew, used family journals and legal records to document more than 30 years of domestic violence.The abuse became increasingly severe. In 1939, a violent attack left Gatewood with cracked ribs, broken teeth and head injuries. When police arrived, they initially arrested Gatewood after she threw a sack of flour while defending herself. After seeing her injuries, the mayor of her town in West Virginia took her into his home for protection. In 1940, Gatewood obtained a rare legal divorce. She received custody of her three youngest children and supported her family through her own work.Gatewood became interested in the Appalachian Trail in the early 1950s after reading aarticle about Earl Shaffer, who completed the first reported A.T. thru-hike in 1948. She noticed that no woman had completed the entire trail alone and decided to try it herself. Her first attempt in 1953 ended in Maine after she became lost and broke her glasses. For her second attempt in 1955, she changed her strategy. She began in Georgia and avoided the park rangers who had advised her to stop two years earlier. She told her adult children only that she was "going for a hike in the woods. " She did not tell them that she planned to walk the entire Appalachian Trail because she feared they would try to stop her. Gatewood also avoided the expensive and heavy equipment used by many modern hikers. She carried her belongings in a handmade denim sack over her shoulder.She did not carry a sleeping bag, tent, compass or detailed map. Instead, she relied on her knowledge of wild plants and found places to sleep wherever she could, including porch swings, park benches and beds of dried leaves. She walked about 14 miles a day, often starting at dawn and continuing until she was completely exhausted. At times, she even walked faster than Boy Scout groups that tried to accompany her.On 25 September 1955, 146 days after leaving Georgia, Gatewood reached Mount Katahdin in Maine, the northern end of the trail. The final stage was difficult. She had fallen the previous day, broken her glasses, sprained her ankle and bruised her face. Despite these injuries, she continued to the summit, where she sang "America the Beautiful."When reporters asked why she had taken on such a difficult journey at age 67, her answer was simple:Her achievement received national attention. Photographs and trail records preserved by the AMC Library & Archives document her journey and later visits to locations such as Lonesome Lake Hut and Carter Notch Hut. Gatewood did not stop after completing the trail once. In 1957, she walked the Appalachian Trail a second time, becoming the first person to complete the entire route twice. In 1964, at age 76, she completed the trail for a third time, this time hiking it in sections.Her achievement also became an important part of the history of women on the Appalachian Trail. Historical figures from the Appalachian Trail Conservancy show that women made up about 15 percent of successful thru-hikers during the trail's early decades. By 2018, women accounted for more than 33 percent of successful thru-hikers. Gatewood's remarkable 1955 journey helped establish an enduring example of what women could accomplish on one of America's most demanding long-distance trails.
Article Summary: Emma Rowena Caldwell was born on a farm in Gallia County, Ohio. She grew up doing hard physical work with her 14 siblings in a small log cabin. Her father, Hugh Caldwell, was a Civil War veteran who struggled with alcoholism and gambling. At 19, Emma married 26-year-old farmer Perry Clayton Gatewood, the marriage began decades of hardship.

Article Title: In 1933, Lincoln's Crooked House was marked for demolition; work revealed a hidden timber-framed building behind its brick façade and saved it; today it is one of the Cathedral Quarter's most photogra
Article Text:
Lincoln's 'Wonky House' set for redevelopment after funding secured

Demolition order reveals a hidden historic building

Centuries of changes

New threats to the timber structure

A demolition order issued in late 1933 was meant to remove a row of ordinary brick terrace houses at the top of Michaelgate in Lincoln. Instead, the first blows from the demolition crew revealed something unexpected: a 16th-century timber-framed building hidden behind the brick exterior. The discovery stopped the demolition of number 40 Michaelgate. Today, the building is known locally as the Crooked House or Wonky House. The Grade II listed property is one of the most photographed historic sites in Lincoln's Cathedral Quarter, behind only Lincoln Cathedral, Lincoln Castle and the Stonebow in popularity. Historical records and the Historic England listing for the building document how it narrowly escaped destruction during the slum clearances of the 1930s.During the early 1930s, towns and cities across England began large urban renewal programs to remove older and unhealthy housing. In Lincoln, these projects targeted crowded homes near the industrial riverfront and along the steep cobbled streets leading toward the Cathedral district. Local historical records published by It's About Lincoln show that a demolition order was issued in late 1933 for numbers 34, 36, 38 and 40 Michaelgate.At the time, number 40 looked like an ordinary brick terrace house. But when workers began removing its outer walls, they discovered heavy timber framing, curved wooden braces and traditional rendered panels hidden behind the later brick facade. After recognising the building's importance, the owner asked the local council to cancel the demolition order. The Minister of Health later approved the building's preservation. However, under the public health rules of the time, it could no longer be used as a home. The City of Lincoln Council eventually bought the property and carried out restoration work to reveal its original 16th-century character. It remains one of England's oldest buildings owned by a local council.Historic England's national heritage list records that the building has two storeys and two bays, with dressed stone, brickwork and a pantile roof. Although its main timber structure dates from the 16th century, the building has been changed several times over the following centuries. The street-facing side has a replica plank door, along with sliding sash and casement windows. The south gable end still contains original corner posts and curved diagonal timber braces, as well as a separate doorway. The building also has unusual features inside. Former residents reported that a chimney breast had been built around an old tree trunk that was already part of the timber structure. The property is managed in partnership with the National Trust and sits near other historic buildings along Steep Hill, including the 15th-century Harlequin Inn at numbers 21 and 22 Steep Hill.Although the building survived the demolition plans of the 20th century, its timber frame has faced new problems in recent years. Heritage Lincolnshire reports that when damaged exterior render was removed in early 2024, conservation workers found widespread damage caused by death-watch beetles. They also discovered older repairs made with dense cement that prevented the historic timber from breathing properly. To protect the structure, Heritage Lincolnshire began a major conservation project with the City of Lincoln Council. More than £451,000 was raised from organisations including the Architectural Heritage Fund, Investors in Lincoln, the Michael Cornish Charitable Trust, the Swire Charitable Trust and Historic England. Tracy Stringfellow, Chief Executive Officer of Heritage Lincolnshire, welcomed the start of the restoration and said the organisation was pleased to help save the iconic Wonky House. She also said the project would eventually create new holiday accommodation in the historic building.City of Lincoln Council also supported the project. Cllr Naomi Tweddle, Portfolio Holder for Inclusive Economic Growth, said that 40-42 Michaelgate was an important part of Lincoln's heritage and that the funding would help protect and restore the buildings while bringing them back into use. Restoration workers are using traditional limewash on the exposed timber frame to help protect it from future insect damage. When the work is finished, income from the new holiday accommodation is expected to help pay for repairs to the neighbouring 15th-century Harlequin building. The project will also allow its historic rooms to be opened for community use. From almost being demolished as an ordinary terrace house in 1933 to becoming one of Lincoln's best-known historic buildings, the Wonky House has survived nearly a century of changing uses, repairs and conservation efforts. Its latest restoration aims to ensure that its unusual timber frame remains part of Lincoln's historic streetscape for generations to come.
Article Summary: Demolition order issued in late 1933 was meant to remove a row of ordinary brick terrace houses at the top of Michaelgate in Lincoln. Instead, the first blows from the demolition crew revealed a 16th-century timber-framed building hidden behind the brick exterior. The discovery stopped the demolition of number 40 Michaelgate. Today, the building is known locally as the Crooked House or Wonky House.

Article Title: A Maine oyster farm is testing a solar-powered floating conveyor that moves oyster baskets through water and air; one raft is designed for 125,000 oysters a year
Article Text:
3-Dimensional Cultivation of Oysters Automated with Solar Tumbling

How the vertical system works

Testing labor and costs

The project has three main goals:

Build and operate the improved prototype in real coastal conditions and collect performance data.

Track mechanical downtime during three-month operating periods to determine maintenance needs.

Measure the number of labor hours required for every 1,000 oysters harvested and use the results to test farm-efficiency models.

Research support and environmental benefits

Engineers and aquaculture experts in mid-coast Maine are testing a solar-powered floating system that could change how oysters are farmed. The platform uses a vertical conveyor to move oyster baskets between coastal waters and the open air.The system, called 3D-COAST (3-Dimensional Cultivation of Oysters Automated with Solar Tumbling), is designed to produce up to 125,000 oysters each year from a single 8-by-25-foot floating raft. Its goal is to increase oyster production while greatly reducing the physical work required from farmers.The project is led by Luke Saindon, founder of Maine aquaculture company The World's Your Oyster Co. (TWIYO), with help from regional scientific institutions.Funding records from the Northeast Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education (NE SARE) program show that $29,978 was awarded in 2025 under USDA project subaward FNE25-131. The funding supports the construction and testing of an improved commercial prototype through March 2027.Traditional oyster farming methods often use floating bags or place oysters on the seafloor. These methods require large amounts of horizontal space and regular manual work, including flipping the bags to control unwanted marine growth.The 3D-COAST raft uses about 12 feet of water depth instead. Oyster baskets are attached to a vertical conveyor loop that is powered by two solar panels.The conveyor completes a full cycle every six hours. As the baskets move, the oysters are gently tumbled underwater and then brought to the surface, where they are exposed to sunlight and air.The tumbling helps shape the oysters. As their growing shell edges are chipped, the oysters can develop deeper and more rounded shells, which can receive higher wholesale prices.The regular exposure to air also helps remove unwanted organisms such as barnacles, sea squirts and algae. These organisms can build up on the cages and reduce the flow of water through the mesh.Oyster farming can require a lot of physical labor. Workers often have to lift heavy cages from the water, many of which become even heavier when covered with marine growth.According to project reports filed with SARE, the automated system is designed to reduce this physical work while also lowering operating costs.The current stage of the project is focused on testing how reliable the system is and measuring how much time it can save compared with traditional farming methods.TWIYO has also developed a custom MATLAB production model and desktop software. These tools allow farmers to test different stocking levels, labor requirements and possible payback periods using data collected from the floating raft.The 3D-COAST system has received support from several state and national research organizations.Early testing was supported by FocusMaine and the Maine Technology Institute (MTI). The project later received Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I funding from the US Department of Agriculture (USDA).Other groups providing support or technical assistance include the Island Institute, the Maine Aquaculture Association, Maine Sea Grant and researchers at the University of Maine's Darling Marine Center.The system could also help address the growing competition for space in coastal waters.Because the raft grows oysters vertically instead of spreading them across a large horizontal area, it could produce more oysters in a smaller footprint. This may reduce competition for water space among commercial fishermen, recreational boaters and waterfront property owners. The smaller footprint could also reduce the visual impact of oyster farms.Field testing of the prototype will continue through the 2026 growing season in mid-coast Maine. Final data on reliability, labor savings and overall efficiency are expected in early 2027.
Article Summary: Engineers in Maine are testing a solar-powered floating system that could change how oysters are farmed. The platform uses a vertical conveyor to move oyster baskets between coastal waters and the open air. Its goal is to increase oyster production while greatly reducing the physical work required from farmers.

Article Title: Virginia installed 46 water-control structures across 150 miles of old drainage ditches to re-wet a swamp; restored peat now traps 200,000 metric tons of carbon a year
Article Text:
The Fish and Wildlife Service restored peat wetlands at Great Dismal Swamp National Wildlife Refuge

Restoring water

Volunteers collect native tallgrass prairie seed at Neal Smith National Wildlife Refuge in Iowa.

Water-control structures

Carbon storage

North Carolina’s coastal peatlands are being restored to protect wetlands, reduce wildfire risks and keep carbon stored in the soil. The work is focused on bringing water back to areas that were once drained and altered for farming, timber harvesting and other uses.Peatlands are wetlands whose soils contain large amounts of partly decayed organic matter. They cover only about 3% of the Earth’s surface but store more than twice as much carbon as all the world’s forests, according to The Nature Conservancy. When peat remains wet, it can hold carbon in the soil. But when it dries, it becomes highly flammable and can release large amounts of carbon dioxide when it burns.This makes water management a key part of conservation in coastal North Carolina. Nature-based solutions can improve wildlife habitat while also helping nearby communities through better water quality, recreation and reduced risks from floods and other climate-related threats.One major focus is the Pocosin Lakes National Wildlife Refuge in the Albemarle-Pamlico Peninsula. The refuge is one of nine national wildlife refuges in the area, which supports fishing and tourism but faces threats from sea-level rise, storms, flooding and wildfires.With funding from the Inflation Reduction Act, the Fish and Wildlife Service and its partners have restored 37,000 acres of peatland at Pocosin Lakes.At Pocosin Lakes, large areas were once crossed by drainage ditches. Centuries of ditching and draining severely degraded peatlands, while earlier land clearing and drainage also affected the refuge.When peat is kept wet, it is less likely to support intense ground fires. "Restoration is focused on rewetting the peat, stopping artificial drainage and restoring or mimicking the natural movement of water across the refuge," Wendy Stanton, manager of Pocosin Lakes National Wildlife Refuge told Public Radio For Eastern North Carolina. She said the restored area now covers more than 37,000 acres.The need for this work became clear during major wildfires. In 2008, lightning started a fire at Pocosin Lakes that burned for three months and destroyed more than 40,000 acres of peat. Meanwhile, the Allen Road fire in 1985 burned through about 100,000 acres, destroyed 26 homes and burned as deeply as three feet into the peat. The fire lasted eight weeks, while an estimated 1 million to 3.8 million metric tons of carbon were released into the air, The Coastal Review reported.Conservation teams are using water-control structures to change how water moves through these drained landscapes. At Pocosin Lakes, the structures can hold back water in drainage systems, helping to restore wetter conditions in the peat. The Nature Conservancy says its teams monitor water levels and adjust the structures to better mimic the natural hydrology of an intact peatland.A similar approach is being used at Angola Bay Game Land. The Nature Conservancy and the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission are working on a restoration design for 7,500 acres of ditched pocosin. Water-control infrastructure began being installed in 2023, with the project also involving plans to restore habitat using wetland species such as Atlantic white cedar, bald cypress, pond cypress and buttonbush.The structures can also be adjusted according to conditions at individual sites. Eric Soderholm, The Nature Conservancy’s coastal wetlands restoration lead in North Carolina, says the approach allows teams to change the effective drainage height by adjusting the boards in the structures. Teams then monitor the results to determine whether water is being held too high or too low.This monitoring is important because the aim is not simply to flood the land. Restoration teams want to create seasonal moisture levels similar to those that would have existed naturally.Keeping peat wet also has implications for climate change. Restored peat wetlands at Great Dismal Swamp National Wildlife Refuge sequester about 200,000 metric tons of carbon each year. That amount is equivalent to the annual emissions of 42,000 vehicles, according to a US Geological Survey and Fish and Wildlife Service study.It estimates that restoring 10 acres of pocosin peatland is comparable to removing the emissions of 5.3 passenger vehicles per year, while draining 10 acres can have the opposite effect.The restoration programme also involves local communities and landowners because changes to water management can affect farms and other livelihoods. Pocosin Lakes has held meetings with surrounding communities to explain its work and hear concerns. Refuge officials have also worked with farmers on drainage issues.The challenge is becoming more urgent as the coastal plain faces rising seas and changing weather. The Pocosin Lakes water management plan notes that the ability of these wetlands to adjust to rising sea levels may be limited if sea-level rise becomes faster than the rate at which peat accumulates.
Article Summary: Peatlands are wetlands whose soils contain large amounts of partly decayed organic matter. They store more than twice as much carbon as all the world’s forests. When peat remains wet, it can hold carbon in the soil. But when it dries, it becomes highly flammable and can release large. amounts of carbon dioxide when it burns.

Article Title: At 20, Finnish immigrant Maggie Walz arrived in Michigan with just $7; in 1903 she claimed 160 acres on a Lake Huron island and the colony she founded grew to five settlements with around 1,000 people
Article Text:
Maggie Walz Photo credit: National Park Service

From servant to entrepreneur

Challenging gender norms

Building a women’s movement

The Walz Block and a personal signature

A colony on Drummond Island

A changing perception

Born Margareeta Johanna Konttra Niiranen in Tornio, Finland, in 1861, Maggie Walz came to the United States at the age of 20 with almost nothing, just $7 in her pocket and a determination to build a new life. According to the National Park Service (NPS), Walz arrived in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula as “a mere girl… a stranger among strangers” in a cosmopolitan settlement of immigrants. She took a job as a domestic servant, learned English through night school, and quickly set her sights on something more. Over the next four decades, Walz would become a pioneering businesswoman, newspaper publisher, suffragette and community builder, challenging the gender norms of her time and leaving an indelible mark on Finnish-American history. Here's her story, as per NPS:After arriving in Michigan, Walz worked for the Jacob Ojanpera family in Oskar, near Houghton. But she had other aspirations. She changed her name to be more readily accepted in mainstream American society and took a job selling sewing machines, pianos and organs door-to-door. Later, she worked as a sales clerk. These experiences helped her master her language skills and taught her the elements of commercial trade.Walz set her sights beyond the Finnish immigrant community, but she was also very active within it.She attended the Finnish Apostolic Lutheran Church, and was a founding member of Pohjantahti (Northern Star), a Finnish temperance society established in Hancock in 1885. She also helped the local Finnish community grow: in 1887, she returned to Finland and came back to the United States with 14 young women immigrants. Walz helped more Finnish women come to the U.S. by underwriting their passage, teaching them English, and helping them find employment. This endeavour led to other business opportunities. She became a ticket agent, a notary public, and opened a currency exchange. She also provided interpretation services for Finnish-speaking immigrants in business, legal, and other transactions for which English was essential.During this era in the Copper Country, women did not typically pursue the professions that Walz chose. By establishing herself as an independent businesswoman, she challenged the notions of women’s proper role in late 19th century society. She was often described as unladylike, if not downright masculine. “She may wear skirts, but she’s no lady!” was an expression commonly quoted in her regard, as per the report. Others said “she had a voice like a sea-captain’s.”Walz’s independent approach to her professional life applied to her personal activities as well. Along with a group of friends, she attempted to establish a women’s suffrage organisation in 1888; their efforts did not meet with much success. Yet Walz was well-regarded, especially in the Finnish immigrant community. Many people owed her a debt of gratitude for helping them make a start in their adopted country long after they had repaid the financial investment she made in their interest.Walz left the Keweenaw to earn a degree in business from Valparaiso College in Indiana. When she returned in 1894, she successfully organised the Calumet Suomen Nais-Yhdistys (Calumet Finnish Women’s Society), which was dedicated more broadly to the general advancement of women, rather than to suffrage alone. It later became a national organisation. The society published a newspaper – the Naisten Lehti (Women’s Paper) – that was eventually distributed nationally. Walz was largely responsible for its publication, serving at various times as business manager, editor, and publisher. At times, Walz produced the paper entirely by herself, and at her own expense. In addition to her work with the Naisten Lehti, Walz was the business manager for another major Finnish-American paper, the Amerikan Suometar, which was also published in Calumet and distributed nationally.In 1902, Walz built a stately, three-story business block on Pine Street, the commercial center of Calumet’s Finnish community. Charles K. Shand, the architect who designed the Red Jacket Opera House (now known as the Calumet Theatre) also designed Walz’s building. The Walz Block housed businesses in two storefronts and other rooms on the ground floor, including the American Suometar business office, and a clothing store operated by Walz herself. Meeting rooms, offices and apartments occupied the upper floors. The pediment of the building announced itself boldly in a stylised inscription designed to look like Walz’s signature, a personalised touch which, though unusual, was perfectly in character for Walz.Walz did not limit herself to the Copper Country: in 1903, she filed a claim under the Homestead Act for 160 acres on Drummond Island, a large island in Lake Huron at the eastern end of the Upper Peninsula. She founded a Finnish colony there in 1905, based on the ideals of temperance, cooperative capitalism, and Christianity. In her honour, the community was named Kreetan, a shortened form of Margareeta, similar to “Maggie” in English. The island colony was a stunning success. The Detroit Free Press reported that as of November 1911, there were “five settlements, with a combined population of probably a thousand.” Education and the creation of community were highly prized and prioritised by any homesteader colony; Kreeton held five stores, a hotel, and the only school attended in the nation attended exclusively by Finnish children. Walz traveled back and forth across the Upper Peninsula for a number of years, maintaining business interests in Calumet as well as on Drummond Island, where she was the postmistress. However, she disassociated herself from the colony when a group of socialists took it over in 1914.By that time, attitudes about women’s rights were shifting. Instead of describing her as unladylike, a Detroit newspaper declared that Walz was “a fine type of independent womanhood, about 40 years of age. She has a good physique and possesses a frank, friendly manner, inspiring confidence in her ability. She is actuated by a desire to benefit her countrymen," as per NPS> The article goes on to list her many business and social accomplishments. This change in perception indicated the arrival of a more modern age that Walz herself may have helped create.Over the next few years, Walz traveled around the United States, establishing branches of Calumet’s Suomen Nais-Yhdistys in other areas. She was active in the Michigan Women’s Christian Temperance Union, and was the American delegate to the International Women’s Christian Temperance Union meeting in Glasgow, Scotland in 1910. She subsequently participated in a women’s delegation to the Coolidge administration in Washington, D.C. As she became increasingly well-known around the country, newspapers began profiling her. Sometimes they referred to her (presumably with the best of intentions) as the “angel of the roundheads,” as Finnish immigrants were somewhat disparagingly known. She was also called the “Jane Addams of Northern Michigan” for her community work.Maggie Walz died in 1927 at the age of 65 at Memorial Hospital in Laurium, where she was being treated for pneumonia. Whether people viewed her as an angel or pioneer of social welfare, one thing is certain: Walz determined her own path in life. After making her way to an unfamiliar country, she proceeded to establish herself in the community. She worked to better the lives of her fellow Finnish immigrants and women in Calumet and beyond. She acted locally, nationally, and internationally to advance women’s rights, and was a powerful advocate for new American citizens.
Article Summary: Maggie Walz came to the U.S. at the age of 20 with just $7 in her pocket. Over the next four decades, she became a pioneering businesswoman, newspaper publisher, suffragette and community builder. Walz was often described as unladylike, if not downright masculine.

Article Title: Manhattan’s got a hairy situation! Giant 10-foot hairball ‘Tumblehair’ takes over the streets of NYC
Article Text:
What was the giant hairball?

Pic courtesy: Instagram/ @uncommon.creative.studio

Breaking the quiet shame

Pic courtesy: Instagram/ @uncommon.creative.studio

Internet's reaction

Pic courtesy: Instagram/ @uncommon.creative.studio

Nothing fazes New Yorkers, or at least that’s what they thought, until they stepped out onto Manhattan streets and encountered a 10-foot sphere of real human hair rolling towards them! A giant 10-foot hairball called Tumblehair rolled through the streets of NYC, leaving pedestrians both repulsed and unable to ignore it.The giant ball was part of a wild marketing stunt created by Uncommon Creative Studio for haircare brand K18, to talk about the “167 billion hairs New Yorkers lose to shedding”. The pedestrians who cussed ‘Eww’ were not wrong. That was gross and disgusting, but according to the studio, the rolling installation highlighted the staggering scale of premature hair ageing and everyday shedding.“We didn’t create a giant Tumblehair just to make you uncomfortable. We wanted to make you stop and think about how much hair you leave behind every day—in your brush, your shower, your drain, and everywhere in between,” the haircare brand said.The art installation rolled across NYC neighbourhoods, including Midtown, West Village, Chinatown and the Seaport. Its final public appearance was at Gansevoort Plaza, and everyone who stopped by got a personal scalp analysis to assess their scalp health, identify concerns and learn how to address them.Hair loss affects roughly 80 million Americans, and two-thirds of men experience noticeable thinning by age 35. Uncommon creative directors Lauren Cooper and Cara Johnson wanted to break the quiet whisper around hair loss. They weren’t ready to approach it ‘quietly and apologetically’ in marketing.“We wanted to flip the script and encourage a conversation about a topic people tend to shy away from, despite many of us experiencing this at some point in our lives. Tumblehair takes something that 80 million Americans are dealing with and makes it impossible to ignore. It’s an absurd visual, but that’s exactly the point,” they said in a statement.The cultural conversation around hair loss is already changing. Hair transplants have become more normalised and more openly discussed. People using hair extensions and wigs do not shy away from talking about it. Even celebrities and athletes speak about it without the old shame. However, marketing firms haven’t caught up to reality yet. Most brands still talk about hair loss the way we discuss other bodily functions: indirectly and euphemistically.The giant hairball rolling through NYC certainly attracted a lot of attention, especially online. The internet split into factions. While some internet users were curious, others were visibly nauseated. “Absolutely no idea what the intention of this hairball is,” one Instagram user wrote.Some users recoiled in horror: “This is so unhygienic.” Some confessed that it made them queasy. Others called it unhygienic and questioned why anyone would want this as an advertisement. “Disgusting, I don’t want to see that as an ad.” A fourth agreed: “This makes me want to throw up.”But some users were genuinely curious. “Am I the only one who thinks it’s cute by the way it moves?” one asked. Some viewers wanted to understand the mechanics. Was it a robot? Was someone inside? “But wait. Is it a robot?! Is someone inside of it?” The most telling reactions came from people who saw themselves in it. “So that’s where all my postpartum hair loss went,” one user quipped.People who found Tumblehair repulsive were still talking about it, still thinking about hair loss, still reacting to something that the industry has spent decades presenting as quietly manageable.Either way, the deliberate, unapologetic campaign, designed to create awareness about hair loss, was impossible to ignore. Maybe that’s the real win. It got people talking!
Article Summary: A giant 10-foot hairball called Tumblehair rolled through the streets of NYC, leaving pedestrians both repulsed and unable to ignore it. The giant ball was part of a wild marketing stunt created by Uncommon Creative Studio for haircare brand K18. It was designed to talk about the “167 billion hairs New Yorkers lose to shedding”

Article Title: In 1905, a 13-year-old crawled through a tiny Tennessee cave passage and found a hidden underground lake
Article Text:
Image: News Channel 9

Meet Ben Sands, the Tennessee teenager who squeezed through a passage no wider than a bicycle tyre

The Lost Sea is 140 feet underground, but its full extent remains a mystery

In 1905, a 13-year-old crawled through a tiny Tennessee cave passage and found a hidden underground lake (Image: Tennessee River Valley)

Before tourists arrived, Craighead Caverns had already witnessed centuries of human history

From a muddy crawlspace to a boat ride across America's largest underground lake

In 1905, a 13-year-old boy exploring Tennessee's Craighead Caverns squeezed through a narrow, muddy passage and stumbled upon something far larger than he could have imagined: a vast chamber containing an underground lake. His name was Ben Sands, and his discovery would eventually become known as the Lost Sea, today recognised as the largest underground lake in the United States. More than a century later, the cavern remains one of Tennessee's most unusual natural attractions, with visitors travelling deep underground to see its enormous body of water. The Lost Sea is an American wonder about 140 feet below the surface. The cave itself has an even older history, with evidence of Indigenous use, Civil War-era mining and other human activity. What began with a curious teenager squeezing through an opening has since become a place where geology, history and exploration converge beneath the Tennessee landscape.The story begins deep inside Craighead Caverns, near Sweetwater in eastern Tennessee. According to CBS News' report, Ben Sands was only 13 when he crawled through a tunnel described by the site's guide as roughly the size of a bicycle tyre. He travelled through the passage for about 40 feet before emerging into a much larger chamber where water reached around his knees.The chamber was so enormous that the light from his lantern could not reveal its boundaries.Sands apparently had no way of knowing how significant the discovery was. To find out how far the cavern extended, he began throwing balls of mud into the darkness. Instead of hitting a wall or the cave floor, they landed in water, producing splashes in different directions. The discovery was especially striking because the lake had effectively been hidden behind a tiny opening. The official history of the Lost Sea similarly records that Sands entered through a small, muddy opening roughly 300 feet underground and found himself in a huge room partly filled with water.The story also illustrates how different the cave was from the attraction visitors know today. The passage Sands entered was considerably smaller when he found it. The route has since been enlarged, allowing visitors to travel through the cavern safely. What was once an almost inaccessible opening became the entrance to one of America's most unusual underground attractions.The body of water discovered by Sands eventually became known as the Lost Sea. It sits approximately 140 feet below ground and is part of the much larger Craighead Caverns system. The visible lake covers about 4.5 acres and measures approximately 800 feet long and 220 feet wide, according to information from the Lost Sea attraction. But calling it a “lake” does not fully capture what lies beneath the visible surface. Explorers and divers have discovered additional water-filled chambers extending beyond the main body of water. The Lost Sea's official records state that more than 13 acres of water have been mapped so far, while the full extent remains unknown. Divers using specialised equipment have explored submerged sections without finding the end of the water-filled system.That uncertainty is part of what makes the Lost Sea unusual. Visitors can see only a portion of a much larger subterranean environment. The lake is at least 70 feet deep and covers around four and a half acres, while modern descriptions of the attraction continue to note that its complete extent has not been established. The Lost Sea is recognised as America's largest underground lake. The U.S. National Natural Landmarks registry describes the Lost Sea cavern system at Craighead Caverns as containing the largest known underground lake in the country. Craighead Caverns has been designated a National Natural Landmark since 1974.The underground lake may be the cavern's most famous feature today, but Craighead Caverns has a much longer human history. The Tennessee State Museum notes that the caves were used by Cherokee people, with archaeological material including projectile points, jewellery and pottery discovered in the cavern system. The cave is named after Chief Craighead, who owned the land in the early 19th century. The caverns later acquired an entirely different role during the Civil War. Confederate soldiers used minerals from the cave to manufacture gunpowder. The official history of the Lost Sea also records that saltpeter was mined inside the cave for this purpose.The cave's cool and stable environment also made it useful for other purposes. Early settlers used portions of it to store food, taking advantage of the naturally cool temperature. Later, different sections of the cavern were used for activities ranging from entertainment to commercial ventures. There are signs that the cave's history stretches much further back than human occupation. The Tennessee State Museum notes that fossilised tracks attributed to a prehistoric jaguar, dating to around 20,000 years ago, have been found within the cavern system. Those traces are now part of the attraction's interpretation of the cave's ancient past.For decades after Sands' discovery, the Lost Sea remained difficult to reach. The tiny passage that had allowed the teenager to enter was not suitable for regular visitors. Eventually, the cavern was developed as a public attraction, with the passage enlarged to make access possible. Today, visitors descend into Craighead Caverns on guided tours before reaching the underground lake. CBS News reported in 2019 that the attraction was drawing roughly 150,000 visitors annually, while the Lost Sea's current visitor information describes a guided cave tour that culminates in a boat ride across the underground lake. The boats allow visitors to experience the unusual scale of the cavern while remaining on the surface of the water.The lake is also home to rainbow trout. CBS News reported that almost 300 trout lived in the underground water at the time of its visit. The unusual environment affects the fish: because they spend their lives in darkness, the attraction's guides have observed gradual reductions in both pigmentation and eyesight. Yet the most remarkable aspect remains the scale of what Sands encountered in 1905. He entered through an opening barely large enough for a child to squeeze through and emerged into darkness that seemed to have no visible end. More than a century later, visitors can now travel through the same underground system in relative comfort, but the essential mystery remains: beneath Tennessee's surface, the water extends into chambers that explorers have still not completely mapped.Ben Sands' discovery therefore sits at the intersection of childhood curiosity and genuine exploration. A teenager following a tiny opening into the darkness uncovered a hidden body of water that would eventually become America's largest underground lake and one of Tennessee's most distinctive natural attractions.
Article Summary: In 1905, a 13-year-old boy exploring Tennessee's Craighead Caverns found a vast chamber containing an underground lake. The lake, known as the Lost Sea, is 140 feet deep and covers around four and a half acres. The cavern has an even older history, with evidence of Indigenous use, Civil War-era mining and other human activity.

Article Title: Hawaii’s 34,000 acres of managed eucalyptus plantations could become a local source of lumber for homes and infrastructure
Article Text:
Image: Canva

Meet the University of Hawaii researchers testing whether local eucalyptus can become construction-grade lumber

Meet the University of Hawaii researchers testing whether local eucalyptus can become construction-grade lumber (Image: Canva)

Why Hawaii has thousands of acres of eucalyptus but still imports construction lumber

How turning eucalyptus into local building material could affect Hawaii’s forests and supply chains

What the eucalyptus research still needs to prove before it can change Hawaii’s construction industry

Hawaii imports much of the lumber used to build its homes, schools and infrastructure, but a new University of Hawaii at Mānoa research project is asking whether some of that material could instead come from trees already growing on the islands. More than 34,000 acres of managed eucalyptus plantations exist across Hawaii, yet much of the wood is not used for structural construction because engineers and builders lack the locally specific design data required to certify it for that purpose. Led by civil engineering researcher Jun Wang, the new project will harvest Hawaii-grown eucalyptus, turn the trees into lumber and test the material for strength and durability. Supported by a $300,000 USDA Forest Service Wood Innovation Grant, the work aims to establish engineering design values for structural applications. The researchers say successful testing could reduce dependence on imported lumber while creating new opportunities for Hawaii’s forestry and wood-products industries.The project is led by Jun Wang, an assistant professor in the University of Hawaii at Mānoa’s Department of Civil, Environmental and Construction Engineering.Rather than assuming eucalyptus is automatically suitable for structural construction, the researchers are taking a testing-based approach: trees will be harvested, processed into lumber and subjected to strength and durability testing so that engineers can establish the numerical design values required for construction. The need for this work is specific to hawaii-grown wood. Earlier U.S. Forest Service research found that eucalyptus grown in Hawaii has useful mechanical properties, but also documented challenges such as growth stress, splitting and differences in density and strength between trees grown in Hawaii and those grown elsewhere. The new research is intended to provide the modern engineering data needed to determine where the locally grown material can safely be used.The University of Hawaii says the project will work with state agencies, forest landowners and industry partners to evaluate the wood under conditions relevant to commercial construction. If the testing establishes reliable design values, the work could eventually support structural applications and engineered wood products made in Hawaii. Wang's broader research focuses on infrastructure sustainability and structural behaviour, making the eucalyptus project part of a wider effort to develop construction approaches suited to Hawaii's environmental and infrastructure needs.Eucalyptus is not new to Hawaii. Different species have been planted on the islands for decades, including Eucalyptus saligna, Eucalyptus grandis and Eucalyptus robusta. The University of Hawaii's College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources notes that E. grandis was introduced to Hawaii in 1957 and is now a major plantation species along the Hāmākua Coast, with wood historically used for poles, construction, mine props and pulpwood. E. robusta, meanwhile, was introduced around 1900 and has been used for house siding, framing, flooring and pallets.The problem is therefore not that eucalyptus has never been used as timber. The problem is establishing the technical evidence required for broader structural use. Building materials have to meet engineering standards that specify how much load they can safely carry and how they behave under different conditions. Without reliable design values for a particular locally available wood resource, builders and engineers cannot simply assume that its performance will match timber produced elsewhere.This issue was recognised decades ago. In a U.S. Forest Service study of 12-year-old Eucalyptus saligna grown on Maui, researcher Roger G. Skolmen found that the trees had potential for lumber but also encountered growth stress and log end-splitting. The resulting lumber was predominantly low grade, although the study found useful properties including relatively high bending strength for its specific gravity and reasonable performance in nailing, machining and glueing.The wood was somewhat different from the same species grown in Australia: Hawaii-grown wood had lower density, shrinkage and compressive strength parallel to the grain, but was approximately equal in bending and shear strength and was stiffer. The researchers described it as exceptionally stiff compared with commercially important mainland species for its density.Those earlier findings help explain why the new project matters. The question is no longer simply whether eucalyptus wood can be sawn into boards. It is whether modern testing can establish sufficiently reliable performance data to allow Hawaii-grown eucalyptus to enter the structural construction market at a much larger scale.If the research succeeds, the benefits could extend beyond replacing imported boards with locally harvested ones. hawaii's distance from major mainland timber-producing regions means construction materials have to travel long distances before reaching the islands. Increasing the use of responsibly managed local timber could shorten supply chains and reduce some of the transport emissions associated with importing lumber. The Hawaii Department of Land and Natural Resources similarly notes that locally sourced wood can reduce shipping-related emissions while supporting local jobs and the state's wood-products economy. The researchers also see a forest-management dimension to the project. The University of Hawaii says greater use of eucalyptus could create an economic reason to manage existing plantations more actively, including removing excess wood that can contribute to wildfire fuel. This does not mean harvesting eucalyptus automatically makes a forest healthier; management outcomes depend on where the trees grow, how they are harvested and what replaces them. But creating a viable market for timber can give landowners another reason to manage plantations rather than allowing usable wood to remain unutilised.That distinction is particularly important in Hawaii because eucalyptus plantations are not the same as native Hawaiian forests. The research is focused on managed eucalyptus plantations, not replacing native ecosystems with commercial tree plantations. The University of Hawaii's forestry resources distinguish between the different eucalyptus species and their management histories, while the current project is specifically concerned with making better use of an existing plantation resource.The potential economic effect could also extend into manufacturing. Once reliable structural properties are established, locally grown timber could potentially be used not only as conventional sawn lumber but as a feedstock for engineered wood products. The University of Hawaii says the current project could lay the groundwork for future engineered wood products made in Hawaii, creating opportunities further down the supply chain for processors, manufacturers and construction companies.The project is still a research effort, not a declaration that Hawaii-grown eucalyptus is ready to replace conventional structural lumber. Researchers first need to establish how the wood performs across the characteristics that matter to construction. That includes strength, stiffness, durability and the consistency of those properties between trees and batches of lumber. The University of Hawaii says the team will produce lumber and test its strength and durability specifically to establish the engineering design values needed for commercial construction.The earlier Forest Service studies demonstrate why that testing cannot be skipped. Growth stress can cause problems during sawing, drying can affect wood dimensions, and different growing conditions can change mechanical properties. The 1974 study of Maui-grown Eucalyptus saligna, for example, recorded average growth stress of about 1,350 pounds per square inch per log and noted that the logs could split badly during processing.The current project is therefore building on a much older body of forestry research while attempting to answer a modern construction question. Its goal is not merely to show that eucalyptus is strong enough for some applications; it is to generate the engineering evidence that allows professionals to calculate safe structural performance. That evidence could ultimately determine whether Hawaii-grown eucalyptus remains primarily a plantation resource used for lower-value products or becomes part of the state's mainstream construction-material supply.The project is also bringing students into the process. The University of Hawaii says Wang's team received an $8,000 American Society for Engineering Education grant to incorporate Hawaii-grown eucalyptus into civil engineering courses. Students will compare the local timber with conventional construction materials while examining structural performance, carbon emissions and local sourcing.For Hawaii, the significance is ultimately larger than one tree species. A locally available material that has long been underused could potentially become part of a more resilient construction supply chain, but only if the science establishes that it can meet the demanding requirements of structural building. The current University of Hawaii project is designed to answer exactly that question. As Wang told UH News, the goal is to determine whether a resource already growing in Hawaii can be used safely to build the homes, schools and infrastructure communities need.If the testing produces the required design values, eucalyptus trees already standing in Hawaii's managed plantations could take on a new role: not simply as forest biomass or a source of limited wood products, but as a locally tested building material capable of contributing to the islands' future construction needs.
Article Summary: Hawaii imports much of the lumber used to build its homes, schools and infrastructure. A new University of Hawaii at Mānoa research project is asking whether some of that material could instead come from trees already growing on the islands. More than 34,000 acres of managed eucalyptus plantations exist across Hawaii. Much of the wood is not used for structural construction because engineers and builders lack the locally specific design data.

Article Title: In 1956, Howard Zahniser began drafting America’s wilderness law; after 66 drafts and eight years of campaigning, he died months before it protected 9.1 million acres
Article Text:
The man who helped define “wilderness,” Howard Zahniser. Image credits: @selwaybitterroot/Instagram

The signing of the Wilderness Act by President Lyndon B. Johnson in September 1964. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

A word nobody could agree on

Howard Zahniser at Spear Falls on the Opalescent River. Image credits:@wyomingwilderness/Instagram

The fine print millennials should actually care about

Why this still matters in 2026

Somewhere in the National Archives lies draft number 66 of a bill that most Americans have never read, yet its language quietly preserves the very landscapes that define the American wilderness today. The person who drafted all these 66 bills did not get the chance to see it turned into law. He missed out on it by just four months.This man was Howard Zahniser, and if you have ever visited national forests, you are benefiting from the legal framework he helped shape. According to The Wilderness Society , Zahniser completed the first draft of the bill that became the Wilderness Act in May 1956, then he spent the next eight years rewriting it 66 times and appearing at 18 different congressional hearings to ensure that it survived. He died of heart failure in May 1964. The Wilderness Act was signed into law by President Lyndon B. Johnson in September of that year, four months too late for Zahniser.Before Zahniser, there was no legal definition of "wilderness" in America. Congress could log it, dam it, or pave it, as long as the multiple-use politics demanded it. Zahniser's solution, which was quite poetic for a legal document, was to define wilderness as land "where man himself is a visitor who does not remain," a line which survived all 66 drafts practically unscathed, as reported by The Wilderness Society.It was one sentence, but it was enough to become the philosophical core of the National Wilderness Preservation System. However, this sentence angered many people. Timber, mining, and grazing interests, as well as the National Park Service and Forest Service, opposed the bill for years because they feared loss of their control over "their" land, as described in a 2014 University of Washington Press article based on the biography of Zahniser written by historian Mark Harvey.Opposition to the bill didn't disappear once Zahniser's language was finalized. In 1960, Congress had passed the Multiple Use, Sustained Yield Act, which some historians describe as a preemptive move by agencies to lock in resource-extraction rights before a wilderness bill could restrict them. Zahniser didn't treat it as a dead end; he spent the next four years continuing to revise his bill and testify before Congress until it passed anyway.When the act was finally signed, 9.1 million acres across 13 different states were put into protection immediately. The legislation banned roads, motorized vehicles, and commercial activities in those areas, and this information comes from a report by the Congressional Research Service published via Congress.gov. Since then, the network has expanded to over 112 million acres, still under the 1964 law.It's easy to mistake this story for a clean success solely traceable to one man's sentence. The reality is far more complex, and it's still worth sitting with the cost behind it: Zahniser spent nearly a decade fighting agencies that wanted his language gutted, watched Congress pass legislation that worked against his goals, and died four months before he got to see any of it signed. The 66 versions drafted by Zahniser show how carefully the wilderness system was written into law. It was protected with painstaking words through legislation by a man who did not get the time to enjoy the fruits of his labor. The fight over wilderness designation continues to this day
Article Summary: Howard Zahniser wrote the first draft of the Wilderness Act in 1956. He spent the next eight years rewriting it 66 times and appearing at 18 different congressional hearings to ensure that it survived. The Wilderness Act was signed into law by President Lyndon B. Johnson in September of that year, four months too late for Zahnisers.

Article Title: '30 civilans killed': Baloch activist shares video of 'Pakistani war crime', seeks US intervention

Mir Yar Baloch has urged the US administration to impose sanctions on Pakistan.

Baloch leader seeks US sanctions

Protests erupt over reported civilian deaths

Mir Yar Baloch, a Baloch leader, has accused Pakistan 's military of carrying out an airstrike in Balochistan that allegedly killed 30 civilians, including women, children and infants.He claimed that video footage from the August 12 attack in Surab's Gidar Goandhan area provides evidence of the military operation and said he plans to take the matter to the International Criminal Court."The Republic of Balochistan has obtained video footage of the Surab Air Strike conducted by the external terrorist forces of Pakistan on 12th August, which killed 30 innocent Balochistan civilians including women, children, and infants and injured dozens more. The missile debris clearly visible in the video constitute irrefutable proof of Pakistan's terrorism. They also thoroughly expose Pakistan's military spokesperson, DG ISPR, who deliberately misled the global community on national media by claiming the attack was merely an IED blast on the ground," Mir Yar Baloch wrote on X.Mir Yar Baloch has urged the US administration to impose sanctions on Pakistan and halt military support, including F-16 engine spare parts and upgrades to fighter jets and missile programmes."The Republic of Balochistan urges the Trump administration to impose strict economic sanctions on Pakistan, cancel the delivery of spare parts for F-16 engines, and halt all upgradation package to its fighter jets and missile program.The Pakistan military and air force are massively employing these very weapons and aircraft against the people of the independent Republic of Balochistan. Washington must hold Pakistan fully accountable for its war crimes in Balochistan," he added.The two sides have given sharply different accounts of what happened in Surab, leaving the circumstances of the incident and the actual civilian death toll disputed.Pakistan's military has rejected the claim of an airstrike and said the casualties were caused by a premature explosion involving a vehicle-borne improvised explosive device allegedly being assembled by militants.The Inter-Services Public Relations said the initial blast killed eight militants and that a secondary explosion involving other explosives stored at the site also caused civilian deaths."However, the blast and secondary detonation of other explosives stored there by the terrorists of Indian Proxy have also reportedly caused tragic casualties of three nearby civilians," the ISPR said.The military said Pakistani forces and Balochistan Police subsequently killed 10 more individuals, taking the reported militant death toll to 18. Two Pakistani soldiers were also injured during the exchange of fire.The competing accounts have come amid protests in Balochistan following reports of civilian deaths in the Surab area.The Balochistan Post reported that more than 20 people were initially killed and at least 16 injured in the incident. Some local residents, however, claimed that the actual death toll could be higher.

Article Title: Why US is questioning Pakistan's Rs 3 trillion defence spending
Article Text:
The US also criticised Islamabad for not publishing its executive budget proposal within a reasonable period (representative image)

US asks Pakistan to improve defence and debt transparency

Pakistan's defence allocation rises to Rs 3 trillion

Defence spending remains a key transparency concern

The US state department has flagged a lack of adequate parliamentary and civilian oversight of Pakistan's military and intelligence spending, while also raising concerns over limited disclosure of government debt and delays in publishing the executive budget proposal.The concerns were highlighted in the 2026 Fiscal Transparency Report, which assessed Pakistan's public financial transparency and identified gaps in the country's budgetary and fiscal disclosure practices.The report noted that Pakistan made its enacted budget and end-of-year financial statements widely available online. However, it said military and intelligence budgets remained outside adequate parliamentary or civilian public scrutiny.“The military and intelligence budgets were not subject to adequate parliamentary or civilian public oversight,” the report said.The US also criticised Islamabad for not publishing its executive budget proposal within a reasonable period.According to the assessment, this limits the time available for lawmakers and civil society to examine government spending before the budget is adopted.The state department called for three key changes to Pakistan's fiscal transparency framework.It urged Islamabad to make its executive budget proposal publicly available within a reasonable period, disclose detailed information about government debt obligations, including liabilities linked to state-owned enterprises, and bring military and intelligence agency budgets under parliamentary or civilian public oversight.The report also raised concerns about Pakistan's disclosure of public debt, saying only limited information was available on debt obligations, including those of major state-owned enterprises.At the same time, the US assessment acknowledged some positive aspects of Pakistan's public financial system.It said the country's supreme audit institution met international standards of independence and noted that its audit reports were published in a timely manner and contained substantive findings.The US assessment comes against the backdrop of a substantial increase in Pakistan's defence allocation for the 2026-27 financial year.In June, Pakistan's federal government proposed allocating Rs 3 trillion for defence services, up 17.65 per cent from the previous year's initial allocation of Rs 2.55 trillion, according to Dawn.The proposed defence services allocation amounts to about 2.08 per cent of Pakistan's projected GDP of Rs 143.6 trillion and nearly 16 per cent of the federal government's total outlay of Rs 18.77 trillion.Spending on civil works related to military infrastructure was projected to rise 7.92 per cent to Rs 363.16 billion, from Rs 336.49 billion previously.Military pensions are accounted for separately from the main defence services budget. The government has allocated Rs 822 billion for retired military personnel under the federal pension outlay, according to Dawn.The allocation for defence administration was set at Rs 10.9 billion, compared with Rs 7.9 billion in the outgoing fiscal year's original budget. That allocation was later revised to Rs 11.75 billion.Major military imports and defence acquisitions are generally funded outside the main defence services allocation and remain undisclosed.The US state department's assessment therefore highlights a distinction between Pakistan's publicly disclosed defence allocation and the wider military spending that may not be fully visible through the country's budgetary documents.The state department's recommendations focus on bringing military and intelligence expenditure into the broader framework of public financial oversight.While the report recognised that Pakistan publishes key budget documents, it identified defence and intelligence spending, debt disclosure and the timing of budget publication as areas requiring greater transparency.The recommendations would require Pakistan to give lawmakers and the public greater visibility into military and intelligence allocations, as well as government liabilities linked to state-owned enterprises.
Article Summary: US asks Pakistan to improve defence and debt transparency. Pakistan's defence allocation rises to Rs 3 trillion for 2026-27 financial year. US state department flagged a lack of adequate parliamentary and civilian oversight of Pakistan's military and intelligence spending. Report also raised concerns over limited disclosure of government debt and delays in publishing executive budget proposal.

Article Title: PML-N set to form 'government' in PoK after two former 'premiers' lose strongholds in third phase
Article Text:
Two former PoK premiers lost their strongholds in the third phase of elections marred by violence and rigging allegations, as the PML-N emerged dominant

Two former so-called prime ministers of Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) lost their traditional strongholds in the third phase of elections, according to unofficial results released on Tuesday, while incumbent premier Faisal Mumtaz Rathore of the Pakistan People's Party (PPP) retained his seat.The latest results came after voting in four constituencies on Monday, with the election process again overshadowed by violence and allegations of rigging. Polling in the remaining seven constituencies was postponed over concerns about the law-and-order situation and is expected to be held on August 21, according to the region's election commission.The PPP won two of the four seats contested in the third phase, while the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and the Awami Dast-o-Bazu Party won one each. The latter is backed by both Jamaat-e-Islami and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).Former prime minister and Muslim Conference president Sardar Attique Ahmed Khan, who was backed by the PML-N, lost the seat in Western Bagh's Dhirkot constituency to Awami Dast-o-Bazu Party candidate Sardar Sajid Iqbal, according to unofficial results. The seat had been held by the Muslim Conference/PML-N since 1985.In Central Bagh, PPP's Zia Qamar retained the seat, defeating PML-N candidate Mushtaq Minhas.Former premier Sardar Tanveer Ilyas, who joined the Istehkam-i-Pakistan Party, secured only a few thousand votes.The result in Eastern Bagh remained pending after authorities ordered a re-poll at 12 polling stations. PML-N candidate Sardar Mir Akbar was leading based on results from 174 of the constituency's 186 polling stations, followed by PPP candidate Sardar Qamaruz Zaman Khan.The election comes against the backdrop of a striking shift in the Pakistani government's treatment of the protest movement that has rocked PoK for months.Just days before the final phase of voting, Pakistan's defence minister Khawaja Asif had described the protesters as "enemies of Pakistan" and ruled out talks with them. But Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's adviser Rana Sanaullah subsequently said 99% of those associated with the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) were "patriotic brothers", promising that a PML-N government would engage with the group and seek to resolve its demands.The reversal in rhetoric came as the PML-N emerged as the dominant force in the election and prepared to form the next government in the region. The party has secured 25 of the 45 directly elected seats so far, while the PPP has won 12 and the Awami Dast-o-Bazu Party one.The first two phases, held on July 27 and August 2, were also marked by violent protests and allegations of widespread rigging, with the PML-N and PPP accusing each other of electoral malpractice. Supporters of the two parties clashed at several polling stations.The JAAC has been protesting across the region since early June, with demands including the abolition of 12 refugee seats that it says can be used to influence the formation of governments in PoK.The group has alleged that more than 40 people were killed during violence surrounding the first phase of voting and that around 400 protesters had been killed since the protests began. The Pakistani government has rejected the higher figure as exaggerated, while Sanaullah has acknowledged that deaths from the unrest were in the "double figures".India does not recognise Pakistan's control over the territory, maintaining that Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh are integral and inalienable parts of India and describing Pakistan's presence in areas under its control as "illegal and forcible occupation".
Article Summary: Two former so-called prime ministers of Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) lost their traditional strongholds in the third phase of elections. Incumbent premier Faisal Mumtaz Rathore of the Pakistan People's Party (PPP) retained his seat. Polling in the remaining seven constituencies was postponed over concerns about the law-and-order situation.

Article Title: 'Discontent answered with bullets': MEA slams Pakistan over PoK crackdown
Article Text:
